polychoice: design document

Source: DESIGN.md

Working title: polychoice (polytomous choice). polytomous was a CRAN package (Arppe, archived 2015-10-29) and the CRAN Repository Policy forbids a name that matches any current or past CRAN package, so it cannot be reused. polychoice, polychotomous, nomchoice, and multichoice were free on CRAN on 2026-10-13. Renaming later is one folder rename plus one sed over DESCRIPTION, R/polychoice-package.R, tests/testthat.R, README, and this file: the name is deliberately kept out of every function and class name (internal prefix .pc_, C++ prefix pc_, S3 base class "choicemodel").

Started 2026-10-13. Sibling of the underdisp (count) and iop (ordered) packages; same author, same engineering conventions, same review protocol. Package and git repository: Underdispersion/polychoice/polychoice/, with this document and verification/ inside it (both excluded from the built package).

“The ledger” below is the author’s working verification ledger, a dated record of every check, review round and stress run. The public repository’s verification/ledger.md summarizes the entries that the vignettes and help pages cite and records the release build’s frozen run; the rest of the working ledger, the stress battery and the one-off probes are kept by the author.

1. Scope

Phase 1 (this build): the MNL core, the inflated MNL, the existing IIA battery

  • mnl(): multinomial / conditional logit by maximum likelihood with case-specific covariates (alternative-specific coefficients), alternative- specific covariates (generic coefficients), alternative-specific constants, varying choice sets, frequency weights, offsets, unit fixed effects (dummies), analytic / robust / cluster-robust / bootstrap covariances.
  • imnl(): the baseline-inflated multinomial logit of Bagozzi and Marchetti (2017, PSRM), generalised to any inflated category and either layout, with a logit or probit split equation; a multistart from the MNL fit.
  • One engine, one object class, one set of methods: print, summary, coef, vcov, logLik, nobs, fitted, residuals, predict, confint, update, simulate, broom (tidy/glance/augment), texreg.
  • Quantities of interest: predict() for observed, outcome-stage, and regime probabilities; first_difference() (delta-method or simulation intervals, with the stage switch of iop); rrr() relative risk ratios.
  • Model fit and comparison: fit_stats() (McFadden, Cox-Snell, Nagelkerke, count and adjusted count R-squared, AIC, BIC), classification(), lr_test(), vuong() (with AIC/BIC corrections), compare_models().
  • IIA / misspecification tests, existing tests only:
    • hausman_mcfadden() (Hausman and McFadden 1984), with the classic variance-difference form and the seemingly-unrelated-estimation joint covariance (Weesie 1999; Stata mlogtest, suest), dropping any alternative including the base (handled by an exact re-basing of the full model).
    • small_hsiao() (Small and Hsiao 1985) in the correct form: full model on both halves, the sqrt(1/2) weighting, restricted model on the second half; optionally repeated over several random splits.
    • fp_tests(): Fok and Paap (2025, J. Choice Modelling) composite-likelihood Hausman test (Q1; default covariance the joint influence-function estimate, F&P’s variance difference as an option, section 5) and GMM overidentification test (Q2; default Hansen’s two-step efficient GMM, the iterated form of F&P and the projected form at the MLE as options), base pairs or all pairs.
    • iia_tests(): the battery in one table.
  • Panel tools: mundlak().
  • Data: pres2004 (Campbell and Monson 2008 as analysed by Bagozzi and Marchetti 2017, Replication II) and pa2006 (Arceneaux and Kolodny 2009, Replication I), so the published fits are regression tests.

Phase 2 (in progress from 2026-10-13, second session)

Done: * Family abstraction: every model shares the design, the beta / gamma blocks, the optimizer, covariances, bootstrap, and methods; a family adds a structural block (internal scale, natural-scale reporting by the delta method) and its own C++ kernel; families without an analytic Hessian use central differences of the analytic gradient in the standardized coordinates. * nlogit(): two-level nested logit in the RU2 / RUM-consistent form of mlogit and Stata; free or shared inclusive-value parameters; singleton nests fixed at 1; exact agreement with mlogit on TravelMode. The nest-level term lambda_m I_m is split as Vmax_m + lambda_m log n_m + O(1) and the nests are compared part by part: the summed form rounded log P to exactly 0 at lambda = e^40 (with equal lambdas and nest sizes the O(lambda) parts cancel and the O(1) parts decide), a false optimum the equal-lambda fit found. mlogit reports BHHH (outer-product) standard errors for the nested logit and HEV; se = "opg" reproduces them, the default remains the observed information. * hev(): heteroskedastic extreme value. Bhat’s Gauss-Laguerre scheme in u = e^{-w} was implemented first and found to converge only algebraically when scale ratios differ from 1 (u^r has a singular derivative at 0 for r < 1): 40 vs 80 nodes differed by 0.5 in a 200-case log-likelihood. Replaced by quadrature in the Gumbel variable w. The log-integrand is strictly concave, so per case and alternative its mode is found by bisection and the window is where the log-integrand has fallen 36 below its maximum (at most 200 units of w either side). When every scale ratio theta_j / theta_k is at most 20 the trapezoidal rule with step 0.35 / r_max converges spectrally (analytic integrand, exponential tails) and is used; a competitor with a much smaller scale makes exp(-h_k) a near step of width 1 / r_k, which a uniform rule needs O(r_k) nodes to resolve, so beyond ratio 20 the window is integrated by adaptive Gauss-Kronrod 7-15 panels (bisect the panel with the largest error until the integrand and two derivative companions are settled to 1e-10; at most 2048 panels), O(log r) panels per step, starting from panels with breakpoints at w*_k + {-4, -1, 0, 1, 4, 12, 40} / r_k around each step w*_k = -a_k / r_k of a competitor with r_k > 1. Checked against R’s integrate() to the test tolerance of 1e-9 for scale ratios up to 1.6e5 (test-families.R). Three earlier rules failed: a window anchored at the root of S(w) = 1 scaled with 1 / theta_j and asked for 1e11 nodes when the optimizer pushed a log-scale towards -20 (a 22 GB process), and a bounded trapezoid grid with the ratio capped at 60 under-resolved the step and let the TravelMode fit run to a spurious optimum at a car scale of 0.004, and the adaptive rule started from uniform 5-unit panels could leave a step in a node-free sliver at the end of a panel after a bisection, where both rules missed it and the error estimate stayed small: the integral came out short by up to 1e-5 at some parameter values and not at others, so the log-likelihood and its gradient jumped and the finite-difference Hessian of the TravelMode boundary fit showed spurious negative curvature (found by the saddle check, 2026-10-14). The error companion of the scale derivative uses sqrt(1 + e^2), not |e| (whose kink sat at the peak of the spike). log P is returned by log-sum-exp, finite where P underflows. mlogit’s HEV is not an oracle: on TravelMode its reported log-likelihood at its own solution is 3.8 above the exact value (ledger), so the kernel is checked against R’s integrate() and the boundary optimum instead. A log scale (or log inclusive value) beyond +/- 7 raises the boundary flag. * mnprobit(): multinomial probit; covariance of the differences from the base through a Cholesky factor with the (1,1) element fixed at 1; exact bivariate normal for three alternatives (ported Drezner-Genz routine from iop), GHK with Halton draws beyond, forward-mode derivatives through the Cholesky differential and the GHK recursion (gradient to 3e-9 of numDeriv with fixed draws; eight times faster than the finite-difference version). Near a singular covariance the GHK simulated likelihood is not smooth: a truncation point is divided by a Cholesky diagonal near zero, so one draw’s term switches between about 0 and 1 over a small change in the parameters (stress finding F24). The boundary warning of a fit with four or more alternatives says so, and the probit’s warning points to vuong(), since lr_test() refuses the probit against the logit. * Further existing tests: combine_test() (Wald and Cramer-Ridder LR), term_test() (Wald / LR per term), hl_test() (Fagerland-Hosmer-Bofin), nested_lm_test() (score test of IIA against a nested logit at lambda = 1), and boot_pvalue() (parametric-bootstrap calibration of a test whose null is the fitted model; round 7 refuses term_test() and combine_test(), whose null is a restriction of it). lr_test() accepts mnl vs nlogit / hev. * se = "opg" (BHHH) for every estimator; simulators rmnl(), rnlogit(), rhev(), rmnp() with gamma (alternative-specific covariates, long-layout output), because the structural parameters of the nested logit, HEV, and probit are weakly identified from case-specific covariates alone (ledger; Keane 1992 for the probit). * Split-panel jackknife for fixed-effects slopes (mnl(fe = , bias_correct = "jackknife"), design below). The gate was redesigned and recalibrated on 2026-10-14: random within-unit placebo splits, kappa = 2.5, alpha = 0.01 (selection rule, selection run, and holdout in the ledger); the jackknife over-corrects at T = 6 and 10 but lowers the RMSE and improves Wald coverage at every T studied (ledger). * Random alternative-specific intercepts: remnl(formula, data, unit, nodes), family "remnl", kernel src/remnl_ll.cpp, implemented as designed below (the observation is the unit: .pc_obs() supplies unit weights and clusters to the covariance code, the bootstrap resamples units and relabels repeated draws, vuong() aggregates an MNL’s contributions over units, lr_test() admits mnl within remnl with a boundary note, the IIA tests refuse non-mnl families). Verification (glmer oracle at J = 2, numDeriv, MNL reduction, recovery) in tests/testthat/test-re.R; results in the ledger. * Four vignettes (getting started; the inflated model; testing IIA and specification; beyond IIA), built with knitr/rmarkdown. Still to do: * The new IIA tests: closed (author’s decision 2026-10-18; section 5.1). Done since: the gate recalibration (2026-10-14) and three rounds of the simulated-referee review (nine perspectives, as for iop), recorded in the ledger.

Designs for the two remaining estimators (written before the code): * Split-panel jackknife (bias_correct = "jackknife" with fe), mirroring underdisp::cpb_fe(): the unit dummies carry an incidental-parameters bias of order 1/T in the slope coefficients; the model is refit on the first and second halves of every unit’s cases (rows split in the order supplied, which should be temporal order) and the corrected slopes are 2 * full - mean(halves) (Dhaene and Jochmans 2015). The half designs are rebuilt from the full design (.pc_half_design()): the fixed-effect columns are regenerated on the subset so never-chosen pairs and empty dummies are handled exactly as in a fresh fit. Validity gate, refusing the correction (returning the ML fit with a warning naming the check) when: the two half-panel slope vectors disagree beyond kappa = 2.5 (calibrated, ledger) times the mean disagreement of five random splits of every unit’s cases into halves of the time split’s sizes (placebo noise, on the time split’s footing under time homogeneity; asymmetric heterogeneity; the first design used five deterministic unit splits with kappa 2.5, then 4), or the full fit’s residuals y_ij - P_ij trend with the within-unit time order for some alternative (Bonferroni over alternatives at 0.01; symmetric heterogeneity, the cure is a time control in the formula). Warns when the median panel length is below 6. Corrected values replace coefficients (slopes only; the unit constants are nuisance), the ML values are kept in $uncorrected, standard errors are the ML ones, logLik refers to the ML fit, and the Monte Carlo of the bias and of the gate is a verification item (size of the refusal on stationary panels, refusal on regime changes). * Random alternative-specific intercepts (re = "unit", family "remnl"): V_ij = … + u_gj for unit g, u_g ~ N(0, diag(sigma_j^2)) over the non-base alternatives, independent across units and alternatives (a correlated version can follow through a Cholesky block). The likelihood is per unit: L_g = int prod_{i in g} P_i(y_i | u) phi(u) du by adaptive product Gauss-Hermite (nodes centred at the mode of each unit’s log-integrand, found by damped Newton, and scaled by the Cholesky factor of its curvature; nodes, default 12 per dimension; a warning above 20000 points), with the log-sum-exp over nodes and the gradient as the mixture-weighted average of the per-node derivatives with the nodes held fixed. The first version used a fixed rule centred at zero; it aliased once the integrand was narrower than the node spacing (long panels, large sigma) and was replaced. The engine’s observation becomes the unit for this family: lli and scores are per unit, frequency weights must be constant within a unit, cluster must nest units, and vuong() against an MNL sums the MNL contributions within units. predict() returns the population-averaged probabilities (integrated over u). Oracles: at J = 2 the model is a binomial GLMM with a random intercept, so lme4::glmer(nAGQ = 25) must be matched to 1e-6 in the log-likelihood and estimates; reduction to the MNL as sigma -> 0; derivatives against numDeriv; recovery; mlogit’s simulated mixed logit (rpar, panel = TRUE) as a loose check at J = 3.

Out of scope: mixed logit with random coefficients (apollo, mixl, gmnl, logitr), Bayesian estimation (MNP, bayesm), ordered alternatives (iop). Ranked alternatives moved into scope on 2026-10-19 (Phase 3).

Phase 3 (from 2026-10-19, author’s decision): captivity, rankings, consideration sets

Status (2026-10-19): A0 done; B (rologit) implemented; A (several inflated alternatives, captivity_test()) implemented; their Monte Carlo studies wait for a frozen build. C stopped at Gate C1, which failed in every design (ledger); the latent consideration-set model is not implemented, and the author decides on any further work. Gate C1 covered case-specific covariates only; a design with a voter-party (alternative-specific) covariate was not tested (see C below).

Designs written before any code. Order of work: (A0) the citation of the captivity literature for imnl(); (B) the rank-ordered logit, the cheapest and lowest-risk; (A) several captive alternatives and the captivity score test; (C) the consideration-set model, which passes two gates before any package code is written. Every item ends with its Monte Carlo study in verification/, run on the frozen build with the rest.

A0. What imnl() is in the discrete-choice literature. The dogit model (Gaudry and Dagenais 1979) adds to the MNL a captive share of the population for each alternative:

P*_ij = (P_ij + theta_j) / (1 + sum_{m in A_i} theta_m),   theta_j >= 0

(P_ij the MNL probabilities over the choice set A_i). With captivity to k only, P*_ik = phi P_ik + (1 - phi), Pij = phi P_ij, phi = 1 / (1 + theta_k): the inflated multinomial logit, and theta_k = exp(-z’ delta) gives phi = Lambda(z’ delta), the logit split equation of imnl() exactly (derived here; Bagozzi and Marchetti’s model with a logit split is the dogit with covariate-dependent captivity to one alternative). Swait and Ben-Akiva (1987a, b) made the captivity parameters functions of covariates (the “parametrized logit captivity” model) as a case of probabilistic choice-set generation. Read 2026-10-19 (the author supplied the papers; ledger): the PLC is their eq. (3) in 1987b, P_i = e^{DX_i} / (1 + sum_l e^{DX_l}) + [1 / (1 + sum_l e^{DX_l})] P{i|C}, captivity odds exp(DX_i) with a constant for every alternative and covariates that may differ by alternative; so imnl() with a logit split is the PLC with captivity to k only, with delta = -D, and several inflated alternatives give the PLC with the same z in every captivity equation. The dogit (their eq. 1) has constant theta_i >= 0 summed over all alternatives; 1987a derives it from independent random constraints (eq. 24). The dogit was proposed as an IIA relaxation: P_ij / P*_im depends on the other alternatives’ utilities. Tse (1987) gives a Lagrange multiplier test of the MNL against the dogit with constant theta (eqs. 4-5, expected information, chi-square on J df, the boundary null read as a test for arbitrarily small theta); the joint statistic of captivity_test() is his, extended to varying choice sets and alternative-specific covariates, and the one-sided z per alternative is added. The documentation cites both papers as such. Bagozzi and Marchetti (2017) cite neither line of work.

B. Rank-ordered logit: rologit(). The exploded logit (Beggs, Cardell and Hausman 1981; Chapman and Staelin 1982; Allison and Christakis 1994; the Plackett-Luce model with covariates). Case i ranks L_i of its available alternatives, r_i1 (most preferred) … r_iL_i; the rest are unranked and tied below the ranked ones (a partial ranking). With R_il = A_i minus {r_i1, …, r_i,l-1}:

log L_i = sum_{l=1}^{L_i} [ V_{i r_il} - log sum_{m in R_il} exp(V_im) ]

with V_ij as in the MNL (stage l is an MNL choice of r_il from R_il; a stage with one alternative left contributes 0). Score: sum over stages of the MNL score of that stage, d log L_i / dV_ij = sum_l 1{j in R_il} (1{j = r_il} - P_ij^(l)); Hessian: minus the sum over stages of the stage covariance of dV/dtheta. Globally concave, as the MNL. * Ties (Allison and Christakis 1994, section 4 and eq. 8, read 2026-10-19): tied alternatives are taken to have an unknown strict order, so a tie group T of d alternatives, ranked above the set B of the alternatives below it, contributes the sum over the d! orders p of T of prod_{s=1}^{d} exp(V_{p_s}) / (sum_{t >= s} exp(V_{p_t}) + sum_{m in B} exp(V_m)). The unranked alternatives form the bottom group, whose term is 1 (no enumeration). This is the exact likelihood; Breslow’s approximation, the default of proportional-hazards software, attenuates the estimates (their Table 1) and is not offered. Middle tie groups larger than 7 are refused (5040 orders). Score and Hessian of a tie group: with l_p the log-probability of order p, g_p and H_p its derivatives in V, and omega_p = exp(l_p) / sum exp(l_q), the group’s derivatives are sum omega_p g_p and sum omega_p (H_p + g_p g_p’) - gbar gbar’. * Interface: long layout only, rologit(rank ~ w | x, data, id, alt, ref, weights, offset, cluster, se, nboot, cores, start, maxit, reltol, depth). The response is the rank: smaller is preferred, any increasing numbers (equal numbers are ties, as Allison and Christakis code them), 0 = unranked (tied at the bottom); a missing rank is a missing value (the case drops, as everywhere). depth keeps only the first depth positions (the alternatives ranked below become unranked; a tie group straddling the cut stays whole), Chapman and Staelin’s explosion depth and Hausman and Ruud’s top-P estimator: both argue, and find in their applications, that later ranks can be noisier (Hausman and Ruud: the pattern depends on the survey). No fe (refused) in this version. * Stability of preferences across ranking stages (the LR test of Hausman and Ruud 1987, section 3, and the Wald form of Allison and Christakis, section 5.4; Chapman and Staelin’s 1982 pooling test is the sequential version, stages 1..E against E + 1; papers read 2026-10-19): rank_test(fit, after = s) refits with separate coefficients for the stages after position s (V_ij^(l) uses theta_late for l > s; within a tie group the position is the order’s own) and reports the LR and Wald tests of equal coefficients. Allison and Christakis note (their footnote 13) that differences between stages can also come from heterogeneity across respondents; the documentation says so. * Implementation: a case-level kernel src/rologit_ll.cpp (lli, gradient, scores, analytic Hessian, probabilities; per case the derivatives are formed in V (a J-vector and a J x J matrix) and mapped to theta through the sparse design rows, as in pc_hess_cpp), on the MNL design with the ranks as an n x J integer matrix in the family’s structural slot; the observation is the case (the ranking), so weights, clusters, bootstrap, vuong() and the covariances need no change. y holds the top choice. predict() returns first-choice probabilities (the MNL over the choice set) and type = "ranking" the probability of the observed ranking; classification() and fit_stats() are about first choices except the log-likelihood-based measures (ranking likelihood; null model: the rank-ordered logit with alternative-specific constants only, or equal probabilities at every stage without constants). simulate() draws rankings (Gumbel utilities), and a simulator rrologit() produces long-layout data with a rank column. The IIA battery, hl_test() and combine_test() refuse a rologit fit; lr_test() and vuong() compare two rologit fits only (a rologit and an MNL fit have different responses). * Oracles: (1) depth = 1 equals mnl() on the first choices exactly (log-likelihood and estimates) when there is no tie at the top; (2) without ties, the exploded data (one pseudo-case per stage, availability R_il) fitted by mnl() give identical estimates and log-likelihood; (3) a tie group’s term equals the brute-force sum over its orders computed in R, and a case whose alternatives are all tied contributes 0; (4) J = 2 is the binary logit; (5) gradient and Hessian against numDeriv, with and without ties; (6) mlogit’s rank-ordered logit where its current version supports it; (7) recovery and coverage Monte Carlo (rologit_mc.R: complete, partial, and tied rankings, J = 4, 5; criteria as recovery_coverage_mc: coverage 0.92-0.98, bias within 3 MC standard errors) and the size of rank_test() under the model.

A. Several captive alternatives (the dogit with covariates) in imnl(). inflate may name several alternatives C (|C| >= 2; logit split only, a probit split is refused with several). Regimes: choose (0) or captive to c in C. With eta_ic = z_i’ delta_c,

pi_i0 = 1 / D_i,   pi_ic = exp(-eta_ic) / D_i,   D_i = 1 + sum_{c in C, a_ic = 1} exp(-eta_ic)
P*_ij = pi_i0 P_ij + 1{j in C} pi_ij

so eta_ic = log(pi_i0 / pi_ic): a positive coefficient makes captivity to c less likely relative to choosing, the reading of imnl()’s split equation, and |C| = 1 is imnl() with the logit link exactly (theta_ic = exp(-eta_ic)). A captive alternative not in a case’s choice set is not a regime for that case (the dogit sums over the choice set; imnl()’s convention for k). Derivatives (derived here; checked against numDeriv and, at |C| = 1, against the imnl() kernel): with the posteriors tau_0 = pi_0 P_y / P*_y and rho_c = 1{y = c} pi_c / P*_y,

dl/dV_j          = tau_0 (1{j = y} - P_j)
dl/deta_c        = pi_c - rho_c
d2l/dV_j dV_m    = tau_0 (1 - tau_0)(1{m = y} - P_m)(1{j = y} - P_j) - tau_0 P_j (1{j = m} - P_m)
d2l/dV_j deta_c  = tau_0 rho_c (1{j = y} - P_j)
d2l/deta_c deta_d = pi_c (pi_d - 1{c = d}) - rho_c (rho_d - 1{c = d})

computed on the log scale (log pi by log-sum-exp over the case’s regimes, log P*_y as a two-term log-sum-exp). * Kernel src/captive_ll.cpp; imnl() with one inflated alternative keeps the existing kernel, so its results do not change. Parameters infl_<alt>:<term> (one block per captive alternative, the same z). Starts as for imnl(), with a binary logit of 1{y != c} on z for each c and common shifts of the intercepts; challengers as for imnl(). Boundary: the existing rules plus a captive share below 1e-6 for every case where c is available (that alternative’s captivity has collapsed; the fit is then the model without it). predict(type = "regime") returns the n x (1 + |C|) regime probabilities, type = "posterior" their posteriors given the choice; rmnl() takes several inflate with a matrix delta. Comparisons: MNL against the captivity model, and the single- against the multi-captive model, are boundary restrictions, calibrated by boot_lr_test(). * Captivity score test captivity_test(mnl_fit, alternatives): the score test of the MNL against the dogit with constant captivity parameters at theta = 0, which is a boundary point in theta but a regular one (the captivity parameterization makes the MNL a finite point, unlike delta at infinity in imnl()). Per-case score s_ij = a_ij (1{y_i = j} / P_ij - 1); information (expected, at the MNL estimate) I_tt[j, m] = sum_i w_i a_ij a_im (1{j = m} / P_ij - 1), I_tb[j, .] = sum_i w_i a_ij (D_ij - Dbar_i)’, I_bb the MNL information, with D_ij = dV_ij / dbeta and Dbar_i = sum_l P_il D_il; efficient information I_tt - I_tb I_bb^{-1} I_bt. Reported: a one-sided z for each alternative (captivity cannot be negative) and the joint LM chi-square. The weights 1 / P_ij make the statistic heavy-tailed when some P_ij are small, so the size Monte Carlo decides whether the normal reference is usable; boot_pvalue() calibrates it in any case. Probe (2026-10-19, before the Monte Carlo; scratchpad): the score equals the numerical derivative of the dogit log-likelihood; under the logit (J = 3, n = 1500, 2000 draws) the z of an alternative whose fitted probabilities reach 3e-4 has skewness 17, IQR-based sd 0.68, 99th percentile 3.07, while its one-sided rejection at 0.05 is 0.042 (0.053 and 0.064 for the other two). So a second form, information = "opg" (the outer product of the per-case efficient scores, summed by cluster when the fit has one), is offered, and the rule for the default is fixed now: the expected form stays the default unless its one-sided size at 0.05 leaves 0.05 +/- 2 Monte Carlo standard errors in some design of captivity_test_mc.R while the opg form’s does not. The documentation reports the size at 0.01 as well. * Oracles and verification: the kernel at |C| = 1 against imnl()’s to 1e-12 (lli, gradient, Hessian); numDeriv; the dogit closed form with an intercept-only split; recovery MC (captive_mc.R: J = 4, two captive alternatives, n = 2000 and 5000, with and without an exclusion restriction; criteria as recovery_coverage_mc, and the shares of boundary fits reported); size and power MC of captivity_test() (captivity_test_mc.R: size under the MNL at n = 500, 2000; power against a single-captive imnl).

C. Consideration sets (latent): gated. Manski’s (1977) two-stage model with independent consideration (the independent-availability model; Swait and Ben-Akiva 1987a; Ben-Akiva and Boccara 1995): alternative j in A_i is considered with probability q_ij = Lambda(z_i’ alpha_j), independently, and the case chooses by the MNL among the considered set C:

P*(y_i = j) = sum_{C subset A_i, j in C} Q_i(C) exp(V_ij) / sum_{m in C} exp(V_im)
Q_i(C) = prod_{m in C} q_im prod_{m in A_i \ C} (1 - q_im) / (1 - prod_{m in A_i} (1 - q_im))

or with alternatives the user declares always considered (abstention, a status quo), which removes the conditioning on a non-empty set. The MNL is the boundary q = 1. Political-science uses: Paap et al. (2005), Oscarsson and Rosema (2019) and that Electoral Studies symposium. The identification results in the economics literature (Abaluck and Adams-Prassl 2021; Barseghyan et al. 2021; the survey of Crawford, Griffith and Iaria 2021) lean on alternative-specific characteristics; with case-specific covariates only (the usual political-science design) the consideration and utility equations are separated only by functional form and exclusion restrictions. Hence two gates before any package code. Corrections after reading the papers (2026-10-19; ledger): Paap et al. use stated consideration sets in estimation (a multivariate probit for consideration, a multinomial probit with a diagonal covariance for the choice, the same respondent covariates in both), but political science also estimates latent consideration sets: Oscarsson and Rosema (2019, p. 260) name Steenbergen and Hangartner (2008), De Vries et al. (2009), and Moral and Zhirnov (2018, AJPS) for that strand (not read here), while recommending direct measures. Of the economics papers, Abaluck and Adams-Prassl identify from asymmetric responses to an attribute that varies across alternatives (prices), Barseghyan et al. give partial identification (point identification needs a restricted choice-set distribution, variation in x, and exclusion restrictions), and Crawford, Griffith and Iaria’s sufficient sets need panel data or groups facing the same choice set; none of them analyses a design with respondent covariates only, so the sentence above is this design’s inference, not their statement. Gate C1 covered case-specific covariates only; designs with a voter-party covariate (an alternative-specific w_ij such as ideological distance), where the economics results apply in spirit, were not tested. * Gate C1 (identification, no fitting): the exact expected information of the model (summing over the J outcomes per case) at designs J = 3, 4, 5, n = 2000, slope sd 0.5 and 1, consideration probabilities averaging 0.6-0.9, (a) z = x, (b) one variable excluded from each side, (c) one always-considered alternative; report the smallest eigenvalue of the normalized information and the standard error of every parameter relative to its true value. Pass: in design (b) or (c), every consideration parameter’s standard error below half its true magnitude at n = 2000. * Gate C2 (recovery, a prototype outside the package): 100 replications at the passing design; pass: median bias of every parameter within 10 percent (or 0.05 absolute), Wald coverage 0.90-0.98, at most 5 percent of fits at a boundary. If C1 fails in every design, the model is not implemented, and the documentation shows instead how a stated consideration set (a survey question) enters mnl() as the choice set; the author decides. * If both pass: kernel src/consider_ll.cpp (enumeration over the 2^(|A|-1) sets containing y, |A| at most 10; the gradient as the posterior-weighted complete-data score; Hessian by differences of the gradient), function consider(), simulator, recovery MC. * Gate C1’ (fixed 2026-10-19, after C1 failed, at the author’s go-ahead; before any computation): the same exact expected information, now on designs with a voter-party covariate, calibrated on real data. Datasets: those of the replication stress test (verification/stress/) that have an alternative-specific covariate varying across voters (a voter-party distance): Alvarez and Nagler (1995), Glasgow (2001), Arzheimer and Evans (2012), and Steiner and Hillen (2021), whichever have their data. In each, the cases, the covariates and the choice sets are the paper’s estimation sample; every alternative-specific covariate is standardized to sd 1 over the available rows. Utility: the paper’s specification, with the true values at the conditional / multinomial logit estimates on that sample. Consideration: logit q_ij = a_j + alpha’ v_ij with an intercept for every alternative not always considered (set so that the mean of q over the cases runs from 0.6 to 0.9 across the alternatives, in level order) and common slopes alpha of magnitude 0.5 and of 1 per sd, negative (more distance, less consideration). Designs: (d) v = the utility’s alternative-specific covariates (the same distances in both equations; the asymmetry identification of Abaluck and Adams-Prassl 2021); (e) v = an alternative-specific covariate excluded from the utility (a second distance in the data, moved from the utility to consideration; skipped where the data have only one); (f) (e) with the paper’s base alternative always considered. Information over the paper’s cases, rescaled to n = 2000 (the information is a sum over cases) and also reported at the paper’s n. Pass (as C1): in some design of some dataset, every consideration parameter’s standard error below half its true magnitude at n = 2000. A pass sends that design to Gate C2; the documentation would then state the designs that pass and those that do not. A failure everywhere closes the latent model. * Gate C2 on the C1’ passes (fixed 2026-10-19 after C1’ passed in 29 of 30 cells, before any C2 run): three designs, each the weakest passing cell of its kind: Alvarez-Nagler (d) alpha -0.5; Glasgow (d) alpha -0.5; Arzheimer (e) with the driving distance to the candidate in consideration only (drdistp), alpha -0.5. 100 replications each at n = 2000: cases drawn with replacement from the paper’s cases, outcomes simulated from the model at the C1’ truth. Fit: maximum likelihood (BFGS, numerical gradient) from two starts, the truth and the conditional logit with every q at 0.8 (alpha = 0), the higher kept; a fit is at the boundary when a consideration intercept exceeds 10 or a slope 10 in magnitude; standard errors from the inverse numerical Hessian. Criteria as C2 above, for every parameter; the Monte Carlo error of each criterion is reported beside it. * Gate C2 result (2026-10-20, ledger): passes in the design with a consideration-only covariate (Arzheimer (e)), fails in both designs where the same distances drive both equations (Alvarez-Nagler (d): 14 percent boundary fits, consideration coverage 0.80-0.91; Glasgow (d): 12 percent boundary fits). The author chose (2026-10-20) to implement the model restricted to designs with consideration-only covariates. * Implementation (fixed 2026-10-20, before any code), within what passed: - consider(choice ~ w | x | v, data, id, alt, ref = NULL, always = NULL, weights, offset, cluster, se, nboot, cores, start, maxit, reltol), long layout only (| 1 | for an empty case-specific part). Utility as in mnl(). Consideration: q_ij = Lambda(a_j + v_ij’ alpha), an intercept a_j for every alternative not named in always (always considered, q = 1) and generic slopes alpha on the columns of v. Every variable of v must vary across the alternatives within cases (a case-specific consideration covariate is identified only through the functional form, Gate C1) and must not appear in the utility parts (the designs that shared them failed Gate C2); both are refused with the reason. The considered set is conditioned to be non-empty when no always-considered alternative is available. No fe (refused). - Parameters: the utility blocks of mnl(), then the structural block “consideration”: consider:<alternative> (the intercepts, in level order) and consider:<column> (the slopes); scales 1 for the intercepts and the column standard deviations over the available rows for the slopes. - Kernel src/consider_ll.cpp: log P*_iy by enumeration over the subsets of A_i that contain y (lli, gradient, scores), all non-empty subsets for the probabilities; |A_i| at most 10 (larger choice sets refused). The gradient as in consider_gate2.R (checked there against numDeriv): omega(C) = Q(C) pi_y(C) / P*_y, dl/dV_m = sum_C omega 1{m in C}(1{m = y} - pi_m(C)), dl/deta_m = sum_C omega (1{m in C} - q_m) - q_m P0 / N (the last term only without an available always-considered alternative); the Hessian by differences of the gradient (the engine’s default). - Starts: the conditional logit on the utility with every free q at 0.6, 0.8 and 0.95 (intercepts at their logits) and zero slopes, each screened and polished (the engine’s multistart). - Boundary: the separation rule of the fit, plus an alternative considered with q > 1 - 1e-6 by every case where it is available (the model without that alternative’s consideration stage), flagged with a warning. - predict(type = "prob") returns P, type = "consideration" the n x J matrix of q (1 for always-considered alternatives, NA where unavailable); simulate() draws from P; simulator rconsider(). - Oracles (tests): with every intercept large (q near 1) the probabilities and log-likelihood equal the conditional logit’s; the probabilities equal the independent R enumeration of Gate C1’ (pstar) and sum to one; the gradient against numDeriv, with and without an always-considered alternative and with varying choice sets. - Recovery Monte Carlo verification/consider_mc.R, fixed now: designs calibrated on real data as in Gate C2, with the package’s own starts (no start at the truth): (A) Arzheimer (e), drdistp in consideration, alpha -0.5; (B) Glasgow (e) with disdef moved to consideration (its weakest (e) cell in C1’), alpha -0.5; (C) Glasgow (f), the same with the base (Alliance) always considered. 200 replications each at n = 2000. Criteria as Gate C2 (median bias within 10 percent or 0.05, coverage 0.90-0.98, at most 5 percent boundary fits), with their Monte Carlo errors; the time per fit reported. A design that fails is reported in the documentation as such, and the author decides on the scope. * Recovery result (2026-10-20, ledger): (A) passes; (B) fails (consideration coverage 0.877-0.913, two utility biases; at n = 5000 one consideration interval still covers 0.88); (C) fails on one utility bias. The standard errors are the inverse observed information (checked against numDeriv); the shortfall is weak identification near q = 1. The author dropped the latent model (2026-10-20): consider(), rconsider() and src/consider_ll.cpp are removed (their last state is commit 5d41a66), the recovery study is archived in verification/archive/consider_mc.*, and the documentation shows the stated consideration set entering mnl() as the choice set.

Phase 4 (from 2026-11-05, author’s decision): Firth’s penalty (firth = TRUE)

Definitions fixed 2026-11-05, before any package code. Derivations: the author’s working note (outside the repository); every formula below was checked numerically first (verification/probes/2026-11-05: firth_proto.R, firth_proto_se.R, coxphf_window.R, with their outputs). Motivation: separation (Cook, Niehaus and Zuhlke 2018 for the multinomial logit); the package flags it (boundary, the IIA tests’ separation warnings) but had no remedy.

Scope. mnl() and rologit() gain firth = FALSE. The other estimators get no such argument: in imnl() and remnl() the restricted model sits where the information is singular (phi -> 1, sigma -> 0), so the Jeffreys penalty tends to -Inf there and would bias every comparison with the multinomial logit towards the larger model; nlogit(), hev() and mnprobit() are not canonical (the penalty is not Firth’s adjusted score there, and the GHK likelihood is not smooth). firth = TRUE with fe is refused (and so the jackknife).

The penalized log-likelihood. l(theta) = l(theta) + (1/2) log|I(theta)|, maximized; with D_R the design rows of the alternatives in R, W_R = diag(P_R) - P_R P_R’: mnl() (wide and long, varying choice sets, offsets, frequency weights): I = sum_i w_i D_i’ W_i D_i, the Fisher information (observed = expected). The model is a canonical exponential family, so this is Firth’s (1993) adjusted score exactly (Bull, Mak and Greenwood 2002; Kosmidis and Firth 2011). * rologit(): I = sum_i w_i sum_G D_{R_G}’ Omega_G D_{R_G} over every group G of a ranking (an untied position is a group of one) with an alternative below it, R_G the group and the alternatives below it, d_G its size: Omega_G = W_{R_G} for d_G = 1; for a tie group Omega_G = sum_{S subset R_G, |S| = d_G} pi_S g_S g_S’, where pi_S is the exact tie probability (Allison and Christakis 1994, eq. 8) of S as the top-d set of R_G and g_S = d log pi_S / dV_{R_G}. Untied rankings give Heinze and Schemper’s (2001) penalty for the Cox model stratified by case, each stage’s information given its remaining set (Heinze and Dunkler 2008, p. 6459); the tie term is the expected information of the tie group’s outcome given R_G and d_G, positive semidefinite and independent of which set occurred (the observed information of the tie term is not used: it depends on the set and need not be positive semidefinite). Only the stages the fit uses (depth) enter; under rank_test() the split model’s information. * Gradient (closed forms, derived and checked against numDeriv): per untied stage (1/2) w_i D’ W a with a = h - 2 H P, H = D I^{-1} D’, h = diag(H); per tie group (1/2) w_i D_R’ sum_S pi_S [(g_S’ H g_S) g_S + 2 G_S H g_S], G_S = d^2 log pi_S / dV dV’. Two passes per evaluation: I at the current point, its inverse, then the per-case terms (C++). * Tie groups: pi_S, g_S and G_S by the recursion f(U) = sum_{j in U} f(U  j) lambda_j / (Lambda_R - lambda(U  j)) over the subsets of R_G of size at most d_G (positive terms only; not inclusion-exclusion, which cancels). A group with more than 10^5 such subsets is refused under firth = TRUE, naming the case. * Optimizer: BFGS with the analytic penalized gradient from the usual start, then the Newton polish with the Hessian by central differences of the analytic penalized gradient (no Newton-first: concavity of l* is not known); convergence by .pc_gtol() on the penalized objective; the saddle check on its Hessian. Amended 2026-11-05 during the first tests, before any Monte Carlo: on a completely separated ranking design BFGS’s first steps followed the separated direction far out and stalled on a flat stretch (34.7 where the maximum, confirmed by coxphf and by the gradient, is at 4.6), so a penalized fit now starts with Fisher scoring (the damped Newton iteration with the information I as its curvature, up to 200 steps, the polish’s step cap and step-halving; as Bull, Mak and Greenwood 2002, logistf and coxphf), and BFGS and the polish continue from its endpoint only when it stops short. The restricted and profile maxima use the same scoring.

What the fit reports. coefficients = argmax l; loglik = l at those estimates (the ordinary log-likelihood, below the maximum-likelihood value); loglik_penalized = l; firth = TRUE. Covariances: "analytic" = I(theta_hat)^{-1}, the model’s information at the penalized estimates (as brglm2, logistf and coxphf; Kosmidis and Firth 2011, p. 758); "opg", "robust", "cluster" from the per-case adjusted scores (the score plus the case’s share of the penalty gradient; they sum to zero at the estimate) with that bread; "bootstrap" refits every replicate with the penalty. The separation diagnostic runs on the maximum-likelihood fit of the same design (computed alongside; both log-likelihoods are concave, the tie term by Prekopa’s theorem): the names of its diverging coefficients are stored (separation) and printed, saying that their penalized estimates are determined largely by the penalty. Amended 2026-11-05 in the first tests: a coefficient is reported as separated when the rule flags its maximum-likelihood estimate and that estimate lies more than 3 penalized standard errors from the penalized one (on Cook, Niehaus and Zuhlke’s Model 3 the rule also flagged the constant of an uncentered year of birth, 171.8 against 165.5 with a standard error of 77, which is not separated).

Inference with a penalized fit. * confint(): type = "profile" (the existing type argument gains the value; written method in the first version of this section), the default for a penalized fit: the values c of theta_r with 2 [l(theta_hat) - max_{theta_r = c} l(theta)] <= qchisq(level, 1), the full model’s penalty in both terms (Heinze and Schemper 2002); found by root finding outward from the Wald limits, NA with a warning when no root lies within 50 Wald standard errors. Maximum-likelihood fits keep Wald intervals. * summary(): Wald z from I(theta_hat)^{-1}, with a line naming the penalty and pointing to profile intervals. Rule fixed now: if the Monte Carlo below finds Wald coverage outside [0.92, 0.98] in a design where profile coverage is inside, summary() reports penalized likelihood-ratio p-values instead. * Penalized likelihood ratio (Heinze and Schemper 2001; coxphftest): 2 [l(theta_hat) - max_{theta in Theta_0} l(theta)], the restricted maximum taken over the full model’s penalized log-likelihood (two separately penalized fits do not give it: their penalties differ). Used by the LR forms of term_test() (the term’s coefficients zero) and combine_test() (Cramer and Ridder’s restriction: all coefficients but the constants equal for the two alternatives), by lr_test() for two penalized fits nested by name (the restricted parameters zero; a penalized and an unpenalized fit are refused), and by rank_test() (early equal to late); the Wald forms use I(theta_hat)^{-1}. * Refused for penalized fits, with the reason: hausman_mcfadden(), small_hsiao(), fp_tests(), iia_tests(), nested_lm_test(), captivity_test(), vuong(), boot_lr_test(). * Unchanged: predict(), fitted(), residuals(), first_difference(), rrr(), classification(), hl_test(), simulate(), update(), coef(), vcov(), nobs(); boot_pvalue() refits every replicate with the penalty. The documentation says that the penalty shrinks fitted probabilities towards equality (Puhr et al. 2017). * fit_stats(): the log-likelihood at the penalized estimates and the penalized log-likelihood; AIC and BIC from the former, labelled as not maximum-likelihood information criteria. logLik() the former, with attribute penalized; glance() adds penalized = TRUE; compare_models() marks penalized fits.

Oracles (tests; the reference packages in Suggests, each test skip_if_not_installed). 1. mnl(), case-specific covariates, with and without weights: brglm2::brmultinom() (estimates to its tolerance; standard errors I^{-1}). 2. J = 2: logistf::logistf() on the differenced data (case-specific and alternative-specific covariates): estimates, profile intervals, penalized LR p-values. 3. rologit() without ties (complete, partial, depth = 1, varying choice sets) and mnl() in the long layout: coxphf::coxphf() with each case on its own disjoint time window, Surv(start, stop, event) (reproduces a stratified Cox fit exactly; verified 2026-11-05): estimates, variance, profile intervals (pl = TRUE), coxphftest(); iteration settings raised for separated designs. 4. numDeriv: the penalized gradient (mnl wide and long with weights, offsets and varying choice sets; rologit with partial rankings and ties of two and three). 5. Tie information: the C++ Omega against an independent R enumeration over subsets and orders; Omega = W at d = 1; the subset recursion against the sum over orders. 6. Invariance and identities: fitted probabilities and l* identical across ref; weight duplication; firth = FALSE leaves every existing fit bit-identical (the existing tests unchanged; the stress battery’s mnl and rologit fits rerun and compared bitwise). 7. Separation: finite estimates on a constructed separated MNL and ranking design, and on Cook, Niehaus and Zuhlke’s data (defection, added at the author’s decision of 2026-11-05 after a licence check, CC0 1.0): their penalized Models 3 to 5 (brglm2, from their replication log) reproduce.

Monte Carlo verification/firth_mc.R (fixed now; run on the final frozen build with the rest), 1000 replications per cell: * F1, multinomial logit, J = 3, wide, n = 50 and 200 (after Bull, Mak and Greenwood 2002, Table 6, models 9 and 11): x1 = 1{z1 > 0}, x2 = z2, (z1, z2) bivariate normal with correlation 0.752 (cor(x1, x2) = 0.6), and a null covariate x3 ~ N(0, 1); coefficients (intercept, x1, x2, x3) for alternatives 2 and 3: model 9 (-1.4, 1, 1, 0) and (-1.4, 1, -1, 0); model 11 (-1.4, 2, 1, 0) and (0, 2, 1, 0). * F2, rank-ordered logit, J = 4, n = 100 and 300 cases, complete rankings and the same data cut at depth 1 and 2: constants (0.5, 0.25, -0.25, base 0), a normal attribute (gamma 0.8), a binary attribute with prevalence 0.1 (gamma 1.5) and a null normal attribute (gamma 0). * F3, F2 at n = 100 with ties: in each ranking, independently of the utilities, positions 2 and 3 are merged into a tie with probability 0.3 and positions 1 to 3 with probability 0.1 (a coarsening that does not depend on the order, the exact likelihood’s assumption). * Reported per cell: the share of samples whose maximum-likelihood fit is flagged separated; for the penalized fit, convergence, mean bias, RMSE and median absolute deviation over all samples; maximum likelihood’s over the samples it converges in; coverage of the 95 percent profile and Wald intervals for every coefficient; the size at 0.05 of the penalized LR test (term_test(test = "lr")) of the null coefficient; the time per fit. * Criteria: (a) every penalized fit converges; (b) profile coverage within [0.93, 0.97] for every coefficient at the larger n of F1 and F2 and in F3; (c) the penalized LR test’s size at 0.05 within [0.035, 0.065] in every cell; (d) at the larger n, every penalized estimate’s mean bias within 3 Monte Carlo standard errors or 5 percent of its true value. A cell that fails is reported in the documentation as such, and the author decides on the scope. The summary() rule above is applied from (b)’s Wald column.

Documentation. ?mnl and ?rologit sections on penalized estimation; NEWS; a vignette section with a separated example; the article (a paragraph and the software table). Datasets from published separated analyses only at the author’s decision, after a licence check.

Phase 4b (2026-11-05 evening, author’s decision): an exact separation check, two starts for penalized fits, and the rank-ordered refusal

Written before the code. Motivation (research-note checks of the same day, Research Notes/rologit_firth/checks/, outside the repository): on 240 simulated ranking data sets the engine’s separation rule (.pc_diverge: |theta scale| > 15, or a 0/1 column’s |theta| > 15, with Wald |z| < 1.96) missed one quasi-complete separation (a binary attribute’s coefficient stopped at 11.4 with a standard error of 2.1e4, fit reported converged) and flagged one overlapping data set whose estimates are large and finite (23 to 30); a linear program decided both correctly and agreed with detectseparation on 549 binary data sets. The penalized likelihood can have two local maxima (binary logit examples, research notes section 9). And rologit() refused data in which an alternative is never ranked above another, with or without firth = TRUE and with or without alternative constants, although that is separation (or nothing at all), not non-identification.

Separation check. * Scope: mnl() and rologit() fits without unit fixed effects and without inflation (the conditional, multinomial and rank-ordered logit), fitted with diagnostics (check = TRUE), and the IIA tests’ refits of such designs (amended below); not rank_test()’s split designs. Other families and fixed effects keep the rule .pc_diverge (their scale and nesting parameters and unit constants are outside this criterion). * Criterion: a finite maximum-likelihood estimate exists iff the structure vectors overlap (Albert and Anderson 1984; Speckman, Lee and Sun 2009 for choice models; Sablica, Hornik and Rusch 2026, Theorem 1, for rankings, partial and tied ones included: a tie group is the event that each tied alternative beats each alternative below it). * Structure vectors, in theta coordinates (D_ij: the case-specific block of non-base alternative m equals X_i when j is that alternative, zero otherwise; then the generic part W_ij), for every case with positive weight: mnl(), D_iy - D_il for every other available l; rologit(), D_ia - D_ib for a in a rank group and b in the next one (ties as groups, the available unranked alternatives last; transitivity leaves the cone unchanged). Offsets and positive weights do not enter. Zero rows and duplicates dropped; columns scaled by their largest absolute value. * Linear program (lpSolveAPI): maximize sum_i tau_i subject to s_i’v - tau_i >= 0, 0 <= tau_i <= 1, v free. The cone of separating directions is closed under addition and positive scaling, so one v reaches tau_i = 1 on every comparison that some separating direction makes strictly positive: the optimum counts those comparisons. Overlap iff the optimum is below 0.5; separated comparisons are those with tau_i > 0.5 (reported by case); complete separation iff all comparisons are separated; the reported direction is v normalized (it separates every separable comparison, so it lies in the relative interior of the cone of separating directions), and the separated terms are its coordinates with |v_k| above 1e-8 times the largest. Amended 2026-11-05 at the first full test run and timing, before any Monte Carlo: (a) that program has a variable per comparison, and lp_solve took 2.1 s at 6,000 comparisons and 88 s at 30,000 (multinomial logit, J = 4, K = 18-21; lp_bench.R, kept with the research-note checks), and it returned “infeasible” (status 2, impossible for a program that v = 0, tau = 0 satisfies) on five fits of the test suite (the cabinets conditional logit, TravelMode, a design with covariates scaled by 1e-6, a long-layout bootstrap, a rank_test() fit). The program is now in the K coefficients: maximize the sum of s_i’v over the comparisons not yet found separable, subject to s_i’v >= 0 for all and -1 <= v_k <= 1; the comparisons it makes positive (above 1e-9) are separable, and it is solved again over the rest until it adds none. A separating direction positive on a remaining comparison would make the objective positive, so every separable comparison is found, and the sum of the solutions, positive on all of them, is the reported direction (0.05 s and 0.1-0.7 s on the same designs, the same separated comparisons; no solver failure in the suite). (b) The separated terms are the coefficients not orthogonal to the span of the cone of separating directions, which is the null space of the comparisons no separating direction favours (singular values at most 1e-9 of the largest): every coefficient that moves along some separating direction, which the coordinates of one solution need not show (a vertex can have zero coordinates). (c) Duplicate comparisons are found by sorting, exactly. (d) Applied to the stress battery’s 63 in-scope designs (verification/separation_stress_check.R), the program took up to 27 s (101,249 cases, 202,498 comparisons) and 59 s (777,688 comparisons), against at most 6 s for the fits themselves, so overlap is first sought by a certificate: by Stiemke’s lemma the comparisons overlap iff some u > 0 has S’u = 0, and at any theta the gradient of the log-likelihood is S’u for positive weights u from the fitted probabilities (in mnl() w_i p_il on the choice over l; in rankings without ties the stage probabilities summed along the chain of consecutive comparisons; not with ties, whose gradient is not such a combination). At a maximum-likelihood estimate S’u is near zero; the least-norm correction that makes it vanish (twice) certifies overlap when every corrected weight stays above 1e-12 of the largest and the remaining S’u is at most 1e-9 of sum |S|’u. Otherwise the program decides. The fits pass their estimates (a penalized fit the maximum-likelihood ones of its second start); separation() the fit’s. (e) A re-solve after the objective changes starts from the previous basis; where lp_solve fails from there (status 3 on Kardasheva 2013, where a fresh model solves under six settings) the program is rebuilt once. * Use: (i) in-scope maximum-likelihood fits: the diverging coefficients are the separated terms (replacing .pc_diverge there; an overlapping data set has none, however large its estimates); the warning names the separation type and terms and points to firth = TRUE and separation(); (ii) in-scope penalized fits: separation holds the separated terms (replacing the maximum-likelihood rule with the 3-standard-error distance); (iii) an exported separation(object) returns the full result (overlap, type, terms, direction, separated cases, counts) for any in-scope fit. Errors in the solver fall back to the rule with a warning.

Two starts for a penalized fit. Without a user start, a penalized fit runs from zero (the default) and from the endpoint of the maximum-likelihood fit of the same design (Newton first; when the penalized objective is not finite there, as along a separating direction far out, the point is halved towards zero until it is, at most 60 times), and keeps the higher maximum. If both runs converge to points that differ (largest |theta scale| difference above 1e-3) with penalized log-likelihoods that differ by more than 1e-6 (1 + |l*|), a warning reports both maxima. Reason: in the research-note examples the zero start finds the lower maximum in one design (separated) and the maximum-likelihood start the lower one in the other (not separated). rank_test()’s penalized fit with separate early and late coefficients (started at the fit’s estimates) runs from the split design’s maximum-likelihood estimate as well, under the same rule; the restricted maxima already run from two starts (.pc_firth_restricted).

rologit()’s refusal. The stop for an alternative never ranked above another available alternative is removed. With alternative-specific coefficients it is separation (the alternative’s constant and case-specific coefficients run to minus infinity), which the check reports for maximum likelihood and the penalty handles; without them it is no restriction. The identification check (.pc_identification_check) and the singular information warning remain. mnl()’s check (an alternative chosen only where no other is available) is unchanged.

Amended the same evening, at the author’s decisions after the first tests (before any Monte Carlo): * mnl() without unit fixed effects or inflation no longer refuses an alternative never chosen (or chosen only where no other is available, or only by cases of weight zero): the same separation as in rankings, reported by the check (its constant and slopes; the other coefficients tend to the fit without that alternative) and finite under firth = TRUE. imnl(), nlogit(), hev(), mnprobit(), remnl() and fixed-effects fits keep the refusal: there the alternative’s own parameters (split equation, nests, scales, variances, unit constants) would not be identified at all. * Bootstrap replicates (se = "bootstrap", the bootstrap tests’ simulated responses): a resample in which an alternative with coefficients of its own is never chosen (in a ranking, never ranked above another available alternative, when the model has alternative-specific coefficients) is a failed maximum-likelihood replicate, as before; a penalized replicate is kept (finite). * The IIA tests judge their half-sample and restricted refits of mnl() by the same exact check (.pc_diverging), so one criterion holds wherever an in-scope design is fitted. * Large but finite estimates raise no flag; ?mnl says that their Wald statistics understate the evidence (Hauck and Donner 1977) and points to the likelihood-ratio tests and firth = TRUE.

Amended 2026-11-05 (night), at the first replication for the research note (Poast 2007, outside the repository), before any Monte Carlo: the penalty’s log-determinant and the inverse in its gradient are those of the equilibrated information I_s = I / (d d’), d = sqrt(diag(I)): log|I| = log|I_s| + 2 sum log d and I^{-1} = I_s^{-1} / (d d’). The same quantities; in theta units I carries the covariates’ scales (Poast’s bid covariates run from 0.3 to 1.7e8: reciprocal condition number 1e-18, against 0.02 for I_s), solve() refused it, and the generalized inverse in its place truncated it, so the penalty’s gradient was wrong (by up to 1.7 in the standardized coordinates) and every penalized fit of the archive’s models stopped unconverged. The covariance was not affected: it inverts I in the standardized coordinates. Test: a covariate multiplied by 1e9 in rologit() and mnl() leaves the penalized fit equivariant.

Tests. The check against detectseparation (binary data through mnl() and through rologit() with two alternatives); the two data sets the rule got wrong, kept as fixed data; the log-likelihood nondecreasing along the reported direction; never-ranked-above data (maximum likelihood warns, the penalized fit is finite, the fit without constants is unaffected); the two two-maximum designs (penalized maxima -1.922670 and -0.157299 found, with the warning); the existing tests updated where the separation report changes. The time of the check on the stress battery’s in-scope data sets is measured and reported (not a test).

Phase 4c (2026-11-06, author’s decision): likelihood-ratio statistics from suprema, the parametric bootstrap for rankings, and priors

Written before the code. Motivation: the research note’s analysis of Poast’s (2007) unreported models (Research Notes/rologit_firth/replications/, outside the repository). 1. term_test(type = "lr") on a completely separated maximum-likelihood fit reported LR = 2.50 for a term whose removal leaves the data completely separated. Both suprema are 0; the restricted refit had stopped at -1.25. 2. With about one to three choices per coefficient, the chi-square reference of the likelihood ratio was far off. Bootstrap medians were 13 to 30 on 10 or 11 degrees of freedom; one bootstrap p-value of 0.145 had a chi-square p-value of 0.0003. boot_lr_test() refused rank-ordered fits. 3. Under separation the penalty decides the size of the separated estimates (Rainey 2016). Jeffreys’ prior is one default; it is not independent across coefficients and can move an estimate against the direction of the separation (Beiser-McGrath 2022). Rainey recommends showing the estimates under several priors.

Suprema. The maximum-likelihood forms of term_test(), lr_test(), combine_test() and boot_lr_test() compare suprema of the log-likelihood, not the values where the optimizer stopped. For an in-scope fit (the scope of the separation check): * Overlap: the fit’s maximum (unchanged). * Complete separation: 0. Along the reported direction v every reported comparison is favoured, so every choice probability, and a tie group’s exact probability, tends to one. * Quasi-complete separation. Along v the separated comparisons’ terms vanish, while the others do not change, since v is orthogonal to every comparison it does not favour. The supremum is approached as follows: 1. From the fit’s point, move along v until every separated comparison’s utility difference is at least 40. 2. Re-maximize from there by the engine’s optimizer. 3. Repeat the move and the re-maximization until the log-likelihood rises by less than 1e-10, at most five times.

The value is below the supremum by at most the number of separated comparisons times e^-40 plus the optimizer’s tolerance. * Out-of-scope designs (unit fixed effects, inflation, the other families, rank_test()’s split designs): the fit’s value, as before. There the rule .pc_diverge judges divergence and no direction is available.

A result whose statistic used a supremum in place of a fit’s value says so in its method line.

The parametric bootstrap for rank-ordered fits. boot_lr_test() accepts two nested rologit() maximum-likelihood fits of the same rankings. * Draws. Each replicate draws, for every case, the restricted fit’s utilities plus independent standard Gumbel errors over the available alternatives, and orders them. Each case then gets its observed pattern: the same rank groups, with the same sizes in the same order (a tie stays a tie at its positions), and the alternatives below them unranked. This treats the coarsening (truncation, ties) as independent of the utilities. * Statistic. 2 (sup_full - sup_restricted), with the suprema above. The full refit also starts from the restricted replicate’s estimates embedded in it, so it cannot end below the restricted one. * Separated replicates are kept. The statistic is defined through the suprema, and in small rankings separation is common under the null: in Poast’s subsamples, 121 to 199 of 199 replicates. They are counted in the method line. * Penalized fits are still refused. Their bootstrap needs penalized refits of both models on every replicate and is not part of this phase.

Priors (prior = in mnl() and rologit()). * Constructor: coef_prior(family = c("normal", "cauchy", "t"), scale = 2.5, df = NULL, intercept_scale = 10, autoscale = TRUE), location 0. The defaults are Gelman et al.’s (2008) Cauchy(0, 2.5) for slopes and scale 10 for constants. * Scope and penalty. It is not allowed with firth = TRUE, and has the same scope as firth: mnl() and rologit(), no unit fixed effects. The objective is the log-likelihood plus the log prior density of each coefficient, up to constants: - normal: -(theta/s)^2/2; - t(df): -(df + 1)/2 log(1 + (theta/s)^2/df); - Cauchy: t(1). * Scales. In theta units the scale is s_k = scale_k / c_k. - With autoscale, c_k is twice the standard deviation of coefficient k’s column for a column with more than two values. For a two-valued column it is the difference of the two values. Both are unweighted, over the estimation rows: the cases for a case-specific covariate, the available alternative rows for a generic one. Otherwise c_k = 1. - The constants (the intercept of the case-specific part, which gives the alternative-specific constants) take intercept_scale, with c_k = 1. - scale may be a named vector by coefficient name. A name set there overrides the default scale for that coefficient, so a separated coefficient can carry its own prior (Rainey’s partial prior). An unknown name is an error. * Estimation: as a penalized fit. - Two starts: zero, and the maximum-likelihood endpoint. - Fisher scoring with I(theta) + max(H_k, 0) as the curvature, where H_k is the negative second derivative of coefficient k’s log prior. * Output. - loglik is the log-likelihood at the estimates; loglik_penalized is the maximized objective. - The covariance is (I + H)^{-1} at the estimates: the curvature of the log posterior at its mode, as arm::bayesglm reports. Firth’s fits report I^{-1}, since Jeffreys’ prior is a bias correction, not information. - Where I + H is not positive definite (a t prior far out on a separated coefficient), the covariance is (I + max(H, 0))^{-1} and a warning points to profile intervals. * Inference. As for Firth’s fits, with the prior’s penalty: - profile penalized-likelihood intervals (confint(), the default); - penalized likelihood ratios in term_test(), lr_test() (two fits with the same prior specification) and rank_test(). - The functions that refuse a penalized fit refuse a prior fit the same way. * Separation. It is reported in separation, as for Firth’s fits.

Tests. * Suprema: - a completely separated ranking in which term_test() gives 0 for a term whose removal leaves the data completely separated (the Poast pattern), where the stopping values gave a positive statistic; - a quasi-complete multinomial design whose supremum equals the maximum-likelihood fit of the data with the separated cases removed by hand; - lr_test() between separated fits. * Bootstrap: - boot_lr_test() on two rologit() fits returns p-values in (0, 1]; - the drawn rankings keep each case’s groups; - a seed reproduces the result; - penalized fits are refused. * Priors: - the normal and t modes equal a direct maximization of the log-likelihood plus log prior written in the test, for mnl() and for a tied rologit() design; - the autoscale constants, and named scales; - firth with prior refused; - finite estimates under separation, with profile intervals and penalized likelihood ratios available; - a very large scale reproduces maximum likelihood on overlapping data. * Size check. A size check of the rank-ordered bootstrap is a verification script, run at the frozen run.

Phase 4d (2026-11-06, author’s decisions on the round-5 review and the stress rerun)

Written with the code, before any test of it ran (internal_reviews/round5/ triage.md; the stress comparison in the ledger, 2026-11-06). * Zero comparisons. A comparison whose structure vector is zero (two available alternatives with the same design row in a case: no alternative-specific constants and equal attributes) is favoured by no direction. - It is left out of the linear program and the certificate, as before, but counted (n_zero; n_comparisons now counts every comparison). - With one, the data are at most quasi-completely separated: that choice’s term stays below zero along every direction. “Complete” requires every comparison separated and none zero. - The supremum then comes from the push and refit, which leaves zero rows alone. Phase 4c’s 0 for a design with zero rows was wrong; the round-5 reviewers’ examples have suprema log(1/2), and the LR of a term was 0 where it is 2 log 2. * The separation check’s scaling. - After the columns, every row of the comparisons is divided by its largest absolute entry. This changes neither the cone nor which comparisons are separated, and it makes the program’s 1e-9 tolerance relative to each row. - The overlap certificate projects the weights by a pivoted QR (the residual on the columns), not by the normal equations, which square the condition number. * Suprema for rankings. The push makes every separated consecutive comparison’s utility difference at least 40. The re-maximization and the rounds take up the comparisons a stage also contains (the e^-40 bound is exact for the multinomial logit only). * The saddle step. - When the saddle check of the fit diagnostics finds a saddle, the search restarts from the probe point where the objective fell most along the eigenvector of the most negative eigenvalue, then takes the boundary step. - When that refit ends higher (by more than 1e-8 relative), the fit is redone from its maximum: at most three times, the multistart’s record kept (the saddle among its ends, classified as a saddle, or as a boundary where coefficients diverge there; Phase 4f), with a message. - Otherwise the saddle warning stands, saying that the step did not end higher. - The check and the step run before the bootstrap and before any warning, on the information already computed for the diagnostics. Internal refits (check = FALSE) skip both. - Case: Liou (2024) Table 1 mnprobit() stopped at a saddle 8.47 below the maximum that a step of 0.3 normalized units reaches. * The boundary step tries the structural log-parameters beyond 3 first together, as before. When that lowers the log-likelihood, it tries them one at a time, largest first, each kept with those already kept when the log-likelihood does not fall. * The bootstrap. - Replicate screening treats prior fits as penalized (they keep resamples with a never-chosen alternative, as Firth’s fits do). - Weighted fits’ replicates (multinomial weights) pass the same checks as unweighted resamples. - boot_lr_test(): - Within the separation check’s scope it keeps single-choice replicates with a never-chosen alternative (separation, whose supremum enters), as for rankings. Out of scope they fail, and the error names the commonest cause. - When the restricted fit is separated, the outcomes are drawn from the point its supremum is approached at (the moved point under complete separation, the moved and re-maximized point under quasi-complete), not from where its optimizer stopped. The method line says so. - Each ranking replicate’s seed is set under the session’s generator kinds, so serial and parallel runs agree. * Priors. - The column scales are frequency-weighted over the rows of positive weight, so a weighted fit and its rows repeated by their weights get the same prior. - A scale named for a coefficient the model lacks is ignored with a message (it was an error), so the restricted model of a penalized LR can take the full model’s prior. - lr_test() compares the penalties on the coefficients the fits share: the same family, degrees of freedom, autoscaling, constants’ scale, and scales. - The documentation says: - that the covariates are not centred; - that the covariance is the inverse of the exact curvature, where arm::bayesglm‘s approximate EM reports a related matrix for t and Cauchy priors; - what the Cauchy’s tail allows. * Profile intervals. - A non-finite deviance (an information underflowing far out on a separated coefficient) lies beyond the limit, not a failed bracket. - Each limit is checked by solving the restricted maximum there afresh, from the estimate and from zero. The warning (the interval may be too narrow) is raised when that maximum does not converge or its deviance is more than 1e-3 from the quantile. The points of the search itself start from the previous point’s solution, and one of them stopping short is not reported: on defection such a point, next to a limit, stopped at a scaled gradient of 0.013 (tolerance 0.002), while the limits solved afresh reproduce the quantile to six decimals, as plain optim() does. - rank_test()’s penalized restricted fit warns likewise. * summary() of a penalized fit marks the separated coefficients’ rows [sep] and says that their Wald tests can be far off (Heinze and Schemper 2002); the test to use is the likelihood ratio. Under a prior the note says that Wald tests can have little power (Rainey 2024). (The wording changed in rounds 6 and 7 and after the local review.) * Smaller rules. - combine_test(type = "lr") takes 0 log 0 = 0 (a never-chosen alternative); the Wald warning is for the Wald form only. - captivity_test() and nested_lm_test() warn on separated fits. - mnprobit() refuses more than 21 alternatives up front. - Firth’s tie kernel computes the subsets’ second derivatives only for the gradient, caps their memory at 200 MB, checks for interrupts, and names the case by its position in the estimation sample. - A restricted model with no parameters is evaluated, not optimized. * Monte Carlo. - firth_mc.R gains F4, a design following that in Rainey (2024, section 3.1), at J = 2 and J = 3 (beta_s in {0, +/-2}), with criterion (e): at beta_s = 0 the penalized and the maximum-likelihood ratio (suprema) reject in at most 0.08 of samples. - rologit_boot_size_mc.R gains designs with ties and truncation, alternative-specific constants and a rare binary attribute; B = 99. * Not changed. - A coordinate exactly at the search’s bound stays free (round 5, I6). The reviewer’s >= would hold a coordinate at the bound even where its gradient points inward, to save one Newton iteration. - The quasi-complete re-maximization in the complement of the separating direction (I4) waits for the run that would show a cost. - remnl()’s dependence on the base alternative is documented, not reparametrized.

Phase 4e (2026-11-06, author’s decision): the likelihood-ratio test of captivity

Why. On pa2006 the score test captivity_test() gives z = 0.50 for abstention while the inflated multinomial logit with a constant captive share of abstention, the score test’s own alternative, gains 10.5 in log-likelihood on one parameter (ledger, 2026-11-06). Its expected information is dominated by cases with small fitted probabilities, and along the captive share the log-likelihood is convex at zero. The likelihood-ratio statistic measures the gain itself.

Definitions, fixed before the code: * The model. For an alternative k, the inflated multinomial logit with k inflated and an intercept-only split equation: P(y = k) = (1 - phi) + phi P_k, P(y = j) = phi P_j, phi constant. In the captive odds theta = (1 - phi) / phi >= 0 it is the dogit with captivity to k alone, and the logit is theta = 0. That is a boundary point of the parameter space, but a regular one: the model is smooth in theta at 0, and every other parameter is identified there. The covariate-dependent split, whose slopes are not identified at phi = 1, is not. * The reference distribution. With q further restrictions in the interior (outcome coefficients of the inflated model that the logit lacks), 2 (l_full - l_restricted) is asymptotically the 50:50 mixture of chi-square(q) and chi-square(q + 1) (Self and Liang 1987; chi-square(0) is the point mass at 0). The p-value is 1/2 P(chi2_q >= LR) + 1/2 P(chi2_{q+1} >= LR). With q = 0 it is 1/2 P(chi2_1 >= LR) for LR > 0, and 1 for LR = 0. The link of the split is immaterial: with a constant split, logit and probit parameterize the same phi. * A statistic of zero. The statistic is floored at 0. A value below 1e-6 is the inflated fit reaching the logit itself, at its boundary (phi -> 1), and is reported as 0. A restricted log-likelihood above the full one by more than 1e-6 warns, as lr_test() does. * lr_test(mnl_fit, imnl_fit) accepts the pair when the inflated fit has one inflated alternative and an intercept-only split (y ~ x | 1), the same cases, weights and choice sets, and outcome covariates that include the logit’s. Several inflated alternatives (several boundary parameters, a chi-bar-square whose weights depend on the information) and any split covariate stay refused, pointing to boot_lr_test(). * captivity_test(object, type = "lr"). For each requested alternative, the constant-share inflated multinomial logit is fitted to the logit fit’s own design, with the split block (one intercept) added: the same cases, weights, offsets and choice sets, by imnl()’s search (multistart and challengers). The table holds one row per alternative: the statistic, df 1, and the mixture p-value. There is no joint row (the joint alternative has several boundary parameters, as above). The attribute fits holds the log-likelihoods, captive shares and convergence flags. - An alternative whose inflated fit fails, or that the inflated model refuses (never chosen; two alternatives), gets NA, with the reason. - Unit fixed effects are refused, as in imnl(). Penalized fits are refused, as in every test of captivity_test(). - The score form stays the default: it needs no refits. * Monte Carlo (captivity_test_mc.R). The LR form joins the size designs (under the logit) and the power designs, at the 0.01, 0.05 and 0.10 levels. The documentation reports what it finds. * Tests. The statistic against the difference of an imnl(y ~ x | 1) fit and the logit, on the wide and the long layout and with weights. The mixture p-value against its formula. LR = 0 at a boundary fit gives p = 1. lr_test() gives the same statistic and p-value, and refuses a split with covariates or several inflated alternatives.

Round 6 amendments (2026-11-06, from the round-6 review)

Phase 4e: * Identification. “Every other parameter is identified” is not enough. The share’s score must also not be a combination of the other parameters’ scores: the fitted probabilities of k must vary in a way its constants and slopes cannot absorb. Under a saturated outcome design the information is singular. The share is then reported as NA, with LR 0, p = 1, status “logit” and a note. * Start at the boundary. Each alternative’s search also starts from the logit embedded at the boundary (the logit’s estimates, split intercept 30). When that start ends above imnl()‘s result by more than the tolerance, the fit is redone from it. * Tolerance. max(1e-6, 2e-8 max(1, |l|)) replaces 1e-6, in captivity_test() and lr_test(). * Status. Each fit gets one of four statuses: - “logit”: the inflated fit at phi -> 1 or LR below the tolerance; LR 0, p 1, and no warning; - “interior”: the mixture p-value; - “degenerate”: LR above the tolerance with diverging outcome coefficients or a saddle (the pres2004 mechanism, ledger 2026-11-06). p is NA, with a note pointing to boot_lr_test(); lr_test() warns and gives NA; - “failed”: NA, with the reason. * Diagnostics. fits keeps the inflated fits’ warnings. top_share is the largest single case’s share of the share’s information at the logit, sum over cases of w (1/P_k - 1) over the available cases. A large value points to boot_lr_test(). On pa2006 it is 0.53, and the bootstrap there (ledger) found the mixture adequate. * boot_lr_test() with the constant-split pair reports the mixture p-value as its asymptotic one. * Monte Carlo. The script logs the raw statistic before the floor, the refits below the logit, the degenerate fits, the warnings and top_share. It adds two size designs with small fitted probabilities (coefficients tripled; a rare alternative).

Elsewhere: * Separation. A comparison whose largest entry is at most 1e-10 after column scaling counts as zero, before the rows are scaled, so rounding cannot turn a zero comparison into a separated one.
