The certificate’s positivity is tested in the rows’ own units. * Priors. autoscale with a weight total of at most 2 (normalized or survey weights) is refused. A misspelled coefficient name gets the near matches. * Engine. - The greedy boundary step skips a candidate with |parameter| <= 3. - The saddle step runs only when the fit is checked. - Fits carry diverging, phi_boundary and saddle. * summary()’s [sep] note. It has one wording per penalty (Phase 4d above).

Round 7 amendments (2026-11-06, from the final review round)

  • One rule for the captive statistic (.pc_captive_rule(), shared by lr_test() and boot_lr_test()). It replaces round 6’s rule in lr_test(), which set the statistic to 0 whenever the share collapsed, for any q. With q further restrictions that is wrong: a collapsed fit with q > 0 is the logit with the further coefficients, and its ratio is theirs (probe r7_lr_test_collapse_q1: 0 instead of 54-121 in 8 of 15 data sets). Now:
    • a collapse counts as 0 only when q = 0;
    • a statistic within the tolerance is 0;
    • degenerate means diverging outcome coefficients or a saddle; the split intercept diverges at a collapse and does not count. boot_lr_test() applies the same rule to its asymptotic p-value (NA for a degenerate fit, noted in the method line), with the flags of the point it uses.
  • The LR form’s identification is decided by the score form’s rule, on the share’s information after the logit’s coefficients are partialled out (.pc_captivity_info()), not by the inflated fit’s conditioning.
  • The LR form’s fits.
    • The embedded start is used when the search fails too, and when it ends above the search by more than the tolerance in the ratio’s units.
    • Each fit keeps its own warnings.
    • n_modes is the search’s count.
  • boot_pvalue() draws from the fitted model, so it calibrates only tests whose null is that model. It refuses term_test() and combine_test(), whose null is a restriction of it (probe r7_boot_pvalue_term_test: p.boot 0.55 for a Wald statistic of 185).
  • Zero comparisons. A generic difference within 64 machine epsilons of its operands is set to 0 when the comparisons are built, and a comparison is zero when all its entries are. This replaces round 6’s 1e-10 of the column’s largest entry, which zeroed genuine differences in wide columns and reported false separation (probe r7_separation_edges).
  • The certificate also requires positivity in the scaled units.
  • hl_test() refuses penalized fits.
  • se = "bootstrap" refuses frequency weights totalling at most 2.
  • The prior’s near-match hint is not given for a term that is a variable of the data the model leaves out.
  • Monte Carlo and verification.
    • firth_mc.R gains F5 (40 cases with s = 1), since F4’s five cases carry almost no information.
    • captivity_lr_pa2006_boot.R joins the frozen run.

Local review amendments (2026-11-06, a max-effort code review run locally)

The review’s report and reproductions are in internal_reviews/local_review_2026-11-06/; each fix has a test in tests/testthat/test-localreview.R (findings 1 and 15 on the Liou fixture in test-phase4d.R). * Likelihood ratios with internal refits. term_test(type = "lr") fits the model without the term as the estimators fit a model, multistart and saddle step included (.pc_refit_checked()), and warns when that fit does not converge or still stops at a saddle. On the Liou probit the old refit of the model without human_rights stopped at a saddle (LR 18.90, p = 7.9e-5); with the step it reaches -1152.021 (LR 2.03, p = 0.36). * A saddle step’s maximum joins start_logliks. * Zero comparisons (.pc_sep_struct()): a difference within 64 machine epsilons of the larger of its operands and the column’s typical size (the median of its nonzero absolute values) is zero, so a tie up to rounding stays a tie after centring, and an outlier does not zero genuine differences. * Never-chosen alternatives. - An alternative never chosen, below the chosen one in separated comparisons only, has probability zero at the supremum (.pc_absent_alts()): its case-specific coefficients do not count in the degrees of freedom of lr_test() and term_test(type = "lr"); the output says so. - nested_lm_test() takes it out (its coefficients and any nest it leaves with one alternative). - captivity_test()’s score form does not test an alternative no case chose; the joint statistic is computed on the correlation scale with one eigenvalue rule for its rank and its inverse. - In the separation check’s scope, a resample (se = "bootstrap", boot_pvalue()) with an unchosen alternative is dropped only when the linear program finds it separated. * rank_test() leaves out coefficients that a block of stages does not identify, with a warning and fewer degrees of freedom; a penalized fit is then refused. * The captive rule (.pc_captive_rule(), now used by lr_test(), boot_lr_test() and captivity_test(type = "lr")): a collapsed share silences only the “restricted fit is higher” warning; a statistic above the tolerance stands. boot_lr_test() takes the full fit’s flags from the engine and reports the statistic its p-values use; its replicates use the same tolerance. * Smaller rules. - combine_test() refuses the same alternative twice. - boot_pvalue() leaves an NA replicate statistic out of its row only (attribute n_na). - A failed separation check in a supremum warns. - Profile intervals: the root to 1e-6 of a standard error. - firth = TRUE refuses weights totalling at most 2; the bootstrap’s weight check runs before the fit and covers remnl(). - hl_test()’s degrees of freedom count the groups and alternatives with expected counts. - Prior df is compared numerically. - Firth’s untied stage guards its 64-bit mask beyond 64 alternatives. - .pc_best_fit() skips its further starts for a concave log-likelihood that converged. * summary()’s [sep] note of a Firth fit cites Heinze and Schemper 2002 (the author’s decision). * F6 in firth_mc.R (the author’s decision): the covariates of design 911 of Rainey’s (2024) replication archive, with criterion (f) on the ML LR rate.

Phase 4f (2026-11-10, author’s decision): the record of the search’s ends

Why. n_modes counted the distinct log-likelihoods, rounded to 0.1, of the converged polished fits. An end at which coefficients diverge can meet the gradient criterion (the gradient vanishes along the diverging direction), so it counted as a maximum: on fluvax the count was 3, of which one end has infl_knowledge diverging and the split at one regime for 87 percent of the cases (verification/probes/2026-11-10/nmodes_classify.R and .txt). Rounding could also merge two maxima less than 0.1 apart.

  • The record. Every end of the search (the polished multistart fits, the challengers and the cross-check that are kept, before a saddle step the original search’s, and the reported fit) enters .pc_search_record(). Ends are taken in decreasing order of log-likelihood. Two ends are the same point when their log-likelihoods differ by less than 0.01 and either every estimate differs by less than a tenth of the first’s inverse-information standard error (by less than 0.01 in the standardized coordinates where it has none) or every fitted probability of every case by less than 1e-4 (the estimate test is tried against every point first). The second test is the data’s own: two ends with the same probabilities have the same likelihood whatever their estimates, so they lie on a ridge of non-identification, and the point’s detail says how many ends joined it that way. The end the reported fit came from belongs to the reported point even when the boundary step has moved the fit.
  • Amendment (2026-11-10, author’s decision, before release). As first implemented (build 28b870609bea) the record grouped by the estimates alone. The stress rerun of that build found the saturated designs of DiGiuseppe et al. (2024) (one binary covariate) reported as up to eleven “distinct local maxima” at one log-likelihood: the search ends at different points of a curved ridge, with estimates several units apart and fitted probabilities equal to 1e-8 (the old rounded count said 1). A test on the straight line between two ends would not do, since the log-likelihood falls along the chord of a curved ridge (by up to 25 at the midpoint there). The tolerance 1e-4 is four orders of magnitude above the agreement of the ends on the ridge and a tenth of the last decimal that summary() prints for a probability. The probability test can only merge points the estimate test kept apart; on a simulated saturated design (one binary covariate, J = 3, two inflated alternatives, six seeds at n = 600 and 1500) the count is 1 where the estimate test gave 3 to 11 (verification/probes/2026-11-10/ridge_probe.R, ridge_sim.R and their outputs).
  • The classification, at each point’s highest end, by the rules of the reported fit’s flags (.pc_end_type()), in this order:
    • "boundary": a diverging coefficient (the exact check of separation() where it applies, the size-and-Wald rule otherwise), a structural log-parameter beyond 7, or a split equation at one regime;
    • "saddle": .pc_saddle() on the normalized Hessian over the parameters with curvature;
    • "not converged";
    • "maximum" otherwise (an ill-conditioned information is noted in detail). The reported point takes its type from the fit’s own flags.
  • Amendment (2026-11-12, author’s decision, before release). Maxima whose information is ill-conditioned (reciprocal condition number below 1e-9, or singular) are one point when their log-likelihoods differ by less than 0.01, whatever their estimates and fitted probabilities; the point’s detail counts the ends that joined it that way. Case: Eifert, Miguel and Posner (2010) Table 4, inflated probit split, a weighted fit with 105 parameters at a boundary: four ends typed "maximum" lay within 6e-05 of one another in log-likelihood among boundary and saddle ends at the same level, and the message reported four distinct local maxima (verification/probes/2026-11-12/search_eifert_t4_probit.txt). A nearly flat direction lets the search stop anywhere along it, so neither the estimates nor the probabilities show that such ends are different maxima. Two distinct ill-conditioned maxima at one height would be counted once. The window is measured from the point’s highest end, and only that end’s estimates are kept in search_theta. An end whose reciprocal condition number is just above 1e-9 is not of this kind, so two ends on one flat region with condition numbers either side of 1e-9 stay two points.
  • The count. n_modes is the number of points of type "maximum"; 0 when there is none (a separated logit, a fit at a boundary with no interior maximum found). A penalized fit keeps its count of the two runs’ maxima and no record; refits with check = FALSE keep neither (n_modes NA).
  • What is reported (the author’s decision of 2026-11-10): the highest end of the search, maximum or not. An inflated fit’s message names the maxima when there are several, with the number of other ends, and when the reported fit is not a maximum but a lower end is, it says so and points to search_theta, whose row refits that maximum as start.
  • What does not change. The search, the reported fit, its estimates, log-likelihood, standard errors, flags and warnings, and start_logliks are as before; on twelve fits (three bundled data sets, six replications of the captive design without an exclusion restriction, three logits) they are identical to build 9446ac9410f9 bit for bit. The classification costs one Hessian per point other than the reported one (0.1 to 0.3 s on the bundled data, against fits of 8 to 20 s).

Phase 4g (2026-11-15, author’s decision): the items held for 0.1.1, done before the release

Why. The rerun of the research note’s scripts on build 8dce1271fc30 and the comparisons of 2026-11-13 left a list of known weaknesses (release checklist, “For 0.1.1”). The author’s decision of 2026-11-15 is to fix them before the first release. Each rule below is the one rule for its case.

  1. Profile limits that do not verify are NA (confint() on a penalized fit). The restricted penalized likelihood, with one coefficient held fixed, can have several local maxima when there are few cases per coefficient or the data are separated: on Poast’s (2007) unreported model for 1981 and earlier, winter, with cius (6 events, 11 coefficients) the package’s optimizer from the estimate, the same from zero, and a BFGS search on a likelihood coded from scratch reach three different restricted maxima at the same point, and the deviance along a path of warm starts is not monotone. A number found there is a point on some path and not a limit. The search first follows the path of warm starts, as before. At the limit it finds, the restricted maximum is taken again from three starts (the path’s solution, the estimate, zero). Where the highest of them converged and reproduces the quantile to 1e-3, the limit is reported. Where one of them is higher than the path’s (the path was on a lower branch), the side is searched again with every point’s maximum the highest of the three starts, and its limit is reported when that maximum converged and reproduces the quantile; the second search has no further check, since its maxima are already the highest found. Otherwise the limit is NA, with a warning that names the coefficient. The earlier text (“the interval may be too narrow”) is withdrawn: restricted maxima found by other means put the unverified limits on either side. (Adversarial review of 2026-11-15, finding 3: the first version checked the second search against starts it already contained, and did not search again when the path’s own solution at the limit was the higher one.)
  2. The second start of a penalized fit (Phase 4b). From the endpoint of the maximum-likelihood fit of completely separated data the run can stop short of a maximum (Poast, 1981 and earlier, summer, without cius: largest scaled gradient 6.2 on build beb30c4880b2 and 0.19 on 8dce1271fc30). A run that does not converge is run again from the point of the segment from that endpoint to zero (at 2^-1, …, 2^-30 of the way) where the penalized objective is highest, and the run with the higher penalized likelihood is kept.
  3. The Fok-Paap tests do not depend on the covariates’ units.
    • Q2: the instruments are put on a canonical scale before the moments are formed. The case-specific covariates x are replaced by sqrt(n) Q of the QR decomposition of x over all cases (columns first scaled to unit length), and the differences w_j - w_m by the same for their rows stacked over the pairs. This is a fixed invertible transformation of each pair’s block of moments, so the moment conditions and the GMM estimate are the same; and Q is the same when a covariate is rescaled or, with the constant first, centered, so the moment covariance, its condition number and the directions its generalized inverse drops are the same too.
    • Q2’s degrees of freedom are the rank of the moment covariance minus the number of parameters. With linearly dependent moments the generalized inverse leaves the dependent directions out of the statistic, and they are left out of the degrees of freedom; with no restriction left, Q2 is NA. A warning states the rank.
    • Q1: on a fit with diverging directions, the directions compared are the complement of the diverging ones in the standardized coordinates theta * scale (orthogonality in theta’s own coordinates depends on the units). The contrast is whitened by the Cholesky factor of the maximum-likelihood covariance before the eigenvalues of its covariance are judged, so the directions dropped are the same under any linear reparametrization (units, centering, a factor’s reference level); scaling by the standard errors alone, the earlier rule, is invariant to units only.
    • The composite-likelihood estimator is found by Newton steps that are halved until the composite log-likelihood does not fall, and has converged when a full step has been taken from a Newton decrement below 1e-8 (100 steps at most; stopping before that step left the estimate up to 1e-6 standard errors off and Q1 up to 1e-5 relative, review finding 5). Where its sensitivity matrix is singular by the rule of .pc_inverse() the estimator does not exist and Q1 is NA with a warning: on gehlbach2010_ta4m7 the undamped search ran to 6e39 and reported Q1 = 7.6e80.
    • Q2 is not computed on a fit with diverging directions. Its moment conditions have no finite solution along them, and the moments at the point where the optimizer stopped depend on that point.
    • Neither test is computed when the fit’s information matrix is ill-conditioned on the directions compared (reciprocal condition number of the normalized matrix below 1e-9, the rule of ill_conditioned). The estimate is then determined to few digits along some direction; on the three batteries of Miller (2017) the statistics changed by a factor of more than 30 between the published units, the same times 1,000 and standardized covariates. The condition number does not depend on the units; a covariate far from its origin (nearly collinear with the constant) can bring it below the bound, and the help page says so.
    • A moment covariance that is not singular by the rule and has a normalized reciprocal condition number below 1e-9 draws a warning: the chi-square reference of Q2 can be far off. moment_rcond in the details is that normalized number.
    • A fit that did not converge draws a warning from fp_tests(): the statistics depend on where the optimizer stopped.
    • A Gauss-Newton step of the GMM estimator is taken on .pc_inverse() of its matrix. A singular matrix (generalized inverse) or a step that is not finite is reported in a warning; before, the loop was left without one.
    • Check: the twelve batteries of the stress records whose statistics changed between builds, each in the published units, with the continuous covariates times 1,000, and standardized (verification/probes/2026-11-15/). In the eight where standardizing leaves the model the same, Q1 and Q2 are the same in the three; in the other four they are the same in the first two (the three of Miller 2017 are NA in all three by the rule above).
  4. singular does not depend on where the search stopped. The information of a model with unidentified parameters is singular at a stationary point; away from one, its smallest normalized eigenvalue is of the order of the gradient (differentiate the constancy of the log-likelihood along the unidentified direction twice). Where the search stopped it computed to 3.7e-15 on Windows and to 2.5e-12 on R 4.5.3 under Linux, on either side of the rule’s 1e-13. A fit whose information has a reciprocal condition number below 1e-6 is therefore polished to stationarity before the flag is set: Newton steps on the generalized inverse of the normalized Hessian without its directions below 1e-9 of the largest singular value. The gradient has no component along an unidentified direction, so these steps remove all of it; a weakly identified direction below that bound is not moved. A step is kept when it is below 1e-3 in the standardized coordinates, does not raise the objective and lowers the largest gradient; at most eight are taken. The rule itself (1e-13 at the point reported) is unchanged. The bound of 1e-6 is far above the values seen at fits of an unidentified model (3.7e-15 and 2.5e-12), which met the engine’s own Newton tolerance (largest gradient below 1e-9 of the objective); a point that only meets the convergence tolerance (1e-5 of the objective) can lie farther from the ridge, with a condition number above the bound, and is then not flagged at all, as before (review finding 2). Families without an analytic Hessian and penalized fits are left as they are. The rule on the scores (withdrawn 2026-11-12) is not needed for this.
  5. Wald tests on a singular fit. term_test() and combine_test() (type = "wald") return NA, with a warning, for a contrast that involves parameters the data do not identify: one with a component along a null direction of the information above 1e-6 of the product of the two lengths. The null directions are taken from the information at the estimates, normalized to a unit diagonal (singular values at most 1e-13 of the largest, the directions the generalized inverse drops), and not from the covariance: the range of a generalized inverse scaled back by the diagonal is not the orthogonal complement of the null space, and a bootstrap or sandwich covariance of a singular fit can have full rank (review finding 1). Contrasts of identified parameters are tested as before.
  6. The saddle step’s second start (Phase 4d). Outside the exact separation check, the saddle check covers the coefficients that the size rule flags and their Wald test spares. At a boundary of a covariance a standard error means little: on koyama2025_t4walter (multinomial probit, var:2 at its bound) the information was not inverted before 2026-11-12, the check left those coefficients out, and the step reached -492.6971, converged; with the inverse on the normalized matrix they were checked, and the step reached -492.7201, not converged. The step now starts from both probe points (with and without those coefficients) when they differ, and the refit that ends higher is kept. On that fit it is -492.6971 again.

Not changed: the citations of Rainey (2024). The note on a separated coefficient of a Firth fit cites Heinze and Schemper (2002) only; the remaining citations are for his findings on maximum-likelihood Wald and likelihood-ratio tests and on Wald tests under a Cauchy prior, which stand.

2. Model and parameterisation

Case i = 1..n, alternatives j = 1..J (the levels of the response), base b, availability a_ij in {0, 1} (all ones in the wide layout).

V_ij = o_ij + x_i' beta_j + w_ij' gamma,      beta_b = 0
P_ij = a_ij exp(V_ij) / sum_k a_ik exp(V_ik)

x_i: case-specific covariates (intercept included: the alternative-specific constants), beta_j alternative-specific. w_ij: alternative-specific covariates, gamma generic. o_ij: offset. This is McFadden’s conditional logit with Theil’s multinomial logit as the special case w = 0, which is how Fok and Paap (2025, eq. 2) write it.

Inflation (imnl): s_i in {0, 1}, P(s_i = 1 | z_i) = phi_i = F(z_i’ delta), F logistic (default; Bagozzi and Marchetti 2017, eq. 5) or standard normal. Inflated category k (default: the base):

P*(y_i = k) = (1 - phi_i) + phi_i P_ik
P*(y_i = j) = phi_i P_ij,   j != k

Log-likelihood sum_i w_i log P*(y_i), w_i frequency weights. The MNL is the boundary case phi -> 1 (delta_0 -> +Inf), so MNL vs imnl is a Vuong / AIC / BIC comparison, not a standard LR test (as in the ZiOP literature).

Parameter vector theta (internal and reported order): 1. beta, alternative-major: for each non-base alternative in level order, the p case-specific coefficients, named "<alt>:<term>"; 2. gamma, named "<term>"; 3. delta (imnl only), named "infl_<term>".

Per-case score (C++):

c_i = 1                       if y_i != k
c_i = phi P_ik / P*_ik        if y_i == k
r_ij = c_i (1{j = y_i} - P_ij)                           dlogP*/dV_ij
u_i  = f(eta_i)/phi_i             if y_i != k            dlogP*/deta_i
u_i  = -f(eta_i)(1 - P_ik)/P*_ik  if y_i == k
s_i(beta_m) = r_im x_i;  s_i(gamma) = sum_j r_ij w_ij;  s_i(delta) = u_i z_i

Gradient of the weighted log-likelihood: sum_i w_i s_i. Hessian: central finite differences of the analytic gradient in the column-scaled parameterisation (the iop recipe); robust covariance H^{-1} (sum_i w_i s_i s_i’) H^{-1}; cluster: sum over clusters of the summed weighted scores. All derivatives checked against numDeriv in the tests.

3. Interfaces

Two data layouts, one formula grammar: the parts of the right-hand side are separated by | (package Formula) and the last part is the inflation equation for imnl().

Wide layout (one row per case, the response is the chosen alternative):

mnl(vote ~ educ + age + female, data = d)
imnl(vote ~ educ + age + female | educ + age, data = d, inflate = "abstain")

Long layout (one row per case-alternative pair; id and alt name the case and alternative columns; the response is the 0/1 choice indicator):

mnl(chosen ~ cost + time | income, data = long, id = "case", alt = "mode")
imnl(chosen ~ cost + time | income | income, data = long, id = "case", alt = "mode")

Part 1 of the long layout: alternative-specific covariates with generic coefficients; its intercept means alternative-specific constants. Part 2: case-specific covariates (constant within case; checked), alternative-specific coefficients. Alternatives absent from a case’s rows are unavailable to it. Alternative-specific coefficients on an alternative-specific variable are the interaction w:alt, so no third covariate block is needed.

Common arguments (names follow iop): ref (base alternative; default the first level), inflate (imnl; default ref), link for the split equation ("logit", "probit"), weights, offset, fe, se = c("analytic", "opg", "robust", "cluster", "bootstrap", "none"), cluster, nboot, cores, start, maxit, reltol.

Semantics carried over from iop/underdisp: weights are frequency weights (a fit with weight 2 equals a fit on duplicated rows, in estimates, standard errors, information criteria, Vuong, averaged QoIs); survey (probability) weights are not supported (the robust meat is the frequency-weight form sum w s s’, see mnl.Rd). Rows with a missing value in any model variable are dropped before fitting; object$data holds the estimation rows. A character response is refused (alphabetical ordering hazard). cluster alone selects se = "cluster".

Fixed effects (fe = "unit"): one dummy per unit in every non-base equation. A unit that never chooses alternative j has that dummy at -Inf; the limiting likelihood is the one with j unavailable to that unit, so those rows get a_ij = 0 and the dummy is omitted (message). A unit that never chooses the base likewise has the base unavailable; its constants are then identified only up to a common shift, so one of its dummies is omitted. The common constant of j refers to a reference unit: the first that chose both j and the base, else (breadth first) one that links j to an already anchored alternative, in which case that unit omits the dummy of the alternative it anchors through; an alternative not connected to the base through the units’ choices is refused by name. Captive cases (one alternative available in the data) do not count as choices, cases of weight zero are dropped first, and cases left with a single alternative drop out; dropping cases can change what a unit chose, so the rules and the drop are repeated to a fixed point (in the fit and in every half-panel or bootstrap design), a unit that chose a single alternative drops out entirely and links nothing, and an alternative chosen only by such units (or only in captive cases) is refused with that cause. Without alternative-specific constants nothing is anchored: every unit keeps all its dummies, one fewer for a unit that never chose the base. imnl() refuses fixed effects (author’s decision 2026-10-18, ledger): with a constant per unit in the outcome equations the level of phi is identified only through the mixture’s form, the routine choosers of k drop out, units with few k choices put them all in regime 0 (their constants diverge), and the split coefficients came out 25-42 percent too large at T = 12-20 (imnl_fe_mc, build 1245fc27f8e3; archived; the split intercept at T = 12 by 42 percent, corrected from “25-40” in round 5). The bootstrap of a fixed-effects fit resamples units (a unit drawn twice is two units) and covers the slopes; a replicate whose fixed effects cannot be built counts as failed. Short panels: the incidental-parameters warning, the split-panel jackknife, and remnl() on the Mundlak-augmented formula.

4. Numerical strategy

  • Starting values: MNL from zero (the log-likelihood is globally concave given full column rank and no separation); imnl from fourteen starts (the MNL fit or an MNL down-weighting the inflated cases, with a logit of 1{y != k} on z for delta at full, halved, doubled, tripled or zero slopes and several shifts of the split intercept), screened by a short quasi-Newton run and every one polished (2026-10-20, stress finding F12: a cap of five polished starts let added starts lower the maximum); with one inflated alternative the same search under the other split link, its estimates rescaled by 1.6 and polished under this link (crosscheck = TRUE; not the default, at the author’s decision of 2026-10-20, since it doubles the time again); then challengers rescaling delta by 0.5, 1.5 and 2, repeated from a new incumbent while one improves (at most three rounds). The polished, cross-check and challenger log-likelihoods are stored (start_logliks), the screened ones too (screen_logliks), and the cross-check (crosscheck); the distinct points where they end, each classified, are in search and search_theta, and n_modes counts the local maxima among them (Phase 4f). The challengers run from the best polished fit only, so the search is not monotone in its starts where the split coefficients diverge: the likelihood then has many flat plateaus (each a hard classification of a few cases into the regimes), and which one the challengers reach depends on the incumbent (stress finding F19: two fits, 0.14 and 1.24 units). Such fits are flagged boundary; challenging the best three maxima would remove the dependence at 40 to 100 percent more fitting time, which the author declined (2026-10-21).
  • Optimiser: damped Newton first for the plain MNL (analytic Hessian), BFGS (optim) with the analytic gradient on column-standardised parameters otherwise, then a Newton polish (analytic Hessian for the logit family, finite-difference Hessian of the analytic gradient otherwise), a step accepted when the objective does not increase (within 1e-14 relative), the step capped at 2 standardized units, convergence declared when the largest scaled gradient is below 1e-5 max(1, |ll|) (.pc_gtol(), the one rule of the polish, the separation rule and the search finish below). The search holds the structural log-parameters within +/- 8, the value the boundary step moves them to (.pc_str_bound): a point beyond is evaluated at the bound with a zero gradient in that coordinate, whose Hessian row and column are those of a fixed parameter (stress finding F22). Past the boundary flag the likelihood is usually flat; where it still rises at the bound (the gradient points out of it by more than the tolerance), the boundary warning names the parameter and says that the reported log-likelihood is below the model’s supremum, so a comparison with the restricted model understates it (on Palik et al. 2025 by 0.67 or more; the author chose this over a wider bound, a measured shortfall or no bound, 2026-11-04). Under hev() and mnprobit() BFGS and the Newton polish run in coordinates that measure each non-base alternative’s coefficients in units of the standard deviation of its utility difference from the base, relative to that at the iid start (.pc_search_map(); sqrt((1 + theta_j^2) / 2) and sqrt(Sigma_jj)): where an alternative’s scale runs to infinity its coefficients grow in proportion, a ridge curved in the coefficients and straight in these coordinates (stress finding F23). Convergence is judged in the model’s coordinates; where the search’s point misses the tolerance there, up to 25 Newton iterations in the model’s coordinates finish the polish (Newton in the model’s coordinates alone is ill-conditioned along the ridge, and the search’s gradient, which weighs the coefficients by the utility’s standard deviation, has another tolerance).
  • Time limits: R raises a limit set by the caller (setTimeLimit(), or a timeout built on it) as an error at the next interrupt check and clears it as it fires; every error handler of the package (a failed start, a singular solve, a failed replicate) signals that error again, so the limit stops the fit rather than one attempt, after which nothing would (stress finding F21). In compiled code with interrupt checks (the remnl(), hev() and mnprobit() likelihoods, every 100 cases in the HEV and probit loops) the limit arrives as an interrupt, as does a user’s interrupt.
  • Diagnostics stored on the object, computed from the information matrix whatever the standard errors are: converged (false also at a saddle: a negative eigenvalue of the diagonally normalized Hessian over the parameters not at a boundary, beyond ten times the asymmetry of a finite-difference Hessian over the same parameters, along whose eigenvector the log-likelihood rises by more than the optimizer’s relative tolerance at a step of 1e-3 to 1 normalized units; on the curved flat ridge of an unidentified model the eigenvalue can be slightly negative while the log-likelihood falls both ways, stress finding F18; a negative eigenvalue whose predicted gain the smallest step would show, with the log-likelihood curving down there instead, is reported as an inaccurate Hessian), boundary (a coefficient whose one-SD effect exceeds 15, or a 0/1 column whose coefficient exceeds 15, and whose Wald |z| is below 1.96, a log scale / inclusive value / sd beyond +/- 7, or the inflated model collapsing onto the MNL), ill_conditioned (reciprocal condition number of the normalized Hessian below 1e-9, or a generalised inverse used), the rank check of every design block, and the scale-free identification check of the choice design. singular (2026-11-10, the author’s decision) records that the generalised inverse was used; summary() then says in its footer that some parameters are not identified and that their estimates and standard errors are not meaningful, since their rows in the table look like the others (the stress battery of build 9446ac9410f9 has 208 such fits, 18 of them not at a boundary; a simulated saturated design printed a z of 127 for a split intercept the data do not identify). The generalised inverse is used when solve() fails or the reciprocal condition number of the normalized information is below 1e-13 (.pc_singular_tol; 2026-11-12, the author’s decision). solve() alone refuses only below machine epsilon, and the same exactly singular information computed to less than that on Windows and to 1.8e-15 on Linux (the saturated design of test-search.R, GitHub Actions, 2026-11-12), so the flag differed by platform. In the stress battery of build beb30c4880b2 on Windows, 72 of 734 fits were ill-conditioned but inverted, with reciprocal condition numbers from 4.6e-16 to 1e-9 and no gap; 14 are below 1e-13 (verification/probes/2026-11-12/rcond_band.R, .txt). At 1e-13 the inverse still has two or three correct digits. The flag still depends on the platform for a model whose parameters are not identified. Its Hessian is singular at the maximum only, and near it the reciprocal condition number grows in proportion to the distance: on the saturated design of test-search.R, 3.7e-15 at the Windows fit, 7e-10 at 1e-8 from it, and 2.5e-12 at the fit of R 4.5.3 on Linux (GitHub Actions, 2026-11-12), which is ill-conditioned and not singular by the rule. Such a fit is flagged on every platform, by one flag or the other, and the test accepts either. A rule on the cases’ scores, which are linearly dependent at every parameter value of such a model (verification/probes/2026-11-12/opg_probe.R, .txt), was tried twice and withdrawn after review (2026-11-12, the author’s decision). Dependent scores alone flagged identified fits on few distinct cases, few rankings or few units (a multinomial logit on 1,035 cases in ten cells, standard errors understated up to sevenfold). Restricted to ill-conditioned fits and to directions of near-zero curvature, it still flagged an identified fit made ill-conditioned by its covariate’s units (reciprocal condition number 1.3e-10; slope standard errors 0.11 to 0.78 of the correct ones, which the inverse had given before), and near the 1e-9 bound it dropped some of the unidentified directions only. Near the cutoff the numbers do not tell a model that is not identified from one that is identified and badly scaled, and a wrong call replaces a correct inverse. A candidate for a later release, with those cases as its tests (verification/probes/2026-11-12/scores_rule/). The rule and the generalised inverse are both applied to the normalized matrix (.pc_inverse()), so neither depends on the parameters’ units: the generalised inverse drops the directions below 1e-13 of the largest singular value there and is rescaled, where MASS::ginv()’s default on the unnormalized matrix dropped everything below 1.5e-8 of its largest singular value, identified directions of small curvature among them. A regular matrix is inverted as before; where solve() refuses it though its normalized form is regular (very different scales), the normalized form is inverted and rescaled, so singular is the rule’s answer on every platform. The outer-product covariance inverts its matrix by the same function. glance() returns singular. (Found by the review of 2026-11-12.) The same function inverts, at the author’s decision of 2026-11-12, the other matrices that fell back on a generalised inverse only when solve() refused: the matrix of .pc_quad_form() (the Hausman-McFadden and Q1 statistics, whose degrees of freedom are the rank it returns) and the GMM weight of Q2, both with the tolerance sqrt(eps) on the normalized matrix, so that a direction whose variance is rounding error does not enter a statistic; the composite-likelihood bread of Q1; and the penalty gradient of R/firth.R. Regular matrices are inverted by solve() as before. Not changed: the Wald-type tests do not consult singular (a candidate for a later release).
  • Q1 on a fit with diverging coefficients (2026-11-12, the author’s decision). fp_tests() leaves the diverging directions out of Q1. With N an orthonormal basis of the span of the separating directions (.pc_separation()$span; outside the exact check’s scope, the coordinates the size-and-Wald rule flags) and B a basis of its complement, the composite-likelihood estimator moves in the span of B from the ML fit, both covariances are the inverses of the two information matrices in B’s coordinates, the contrast is B’(theta_ML - theta_CL), and the degrees of freedom are K minus the rank of N. The warning says so, the details name the coefficients that move along N and its rank, and the printed table carries a line. A separated reference cell is one direction through an intercept and its dummies, whose sums stay in the comparison (review of 2026-11-12: leaving out the coefficients would hold those sums at their ML values and lose degrees of freedom).
    • Why. On separated samples the statistic depended on how each inversion treated a direction without information. On 400 samples drawn from the pa2006 multinomial logit, 55 separate (the nonresponse equation on voted2004: one direction). In build beb30c4880b2 solve() refused the unnormalized composite-likelihood bread on them (reciprocal condition number 8e-17 to 2.2e-16), MASS::ginv() then dropped the diverging direction from that estimator’s covariance while the ML covariance kept it, and Q1 was 1,020 to 1,846 on 23 degrees of freedom: every separated sample rejected, and the bootstrap p-value of the observed Q1 was 0.14 (0.26 with the vignette’s 49 replicates). With that direction kept in both covariances or dropped from both, Q1 is 18.1 or 18.2 on a sample where dropping it from one gives 1,188; and the bread’s normalized reciprocal condition number, 8.9e-14 to 2.5e-13, straddles the cutoff of .pc_inverse(), so the inversion alone would not settle it on every platform.
    • Result. The separated samples’ Q1 has mean 20.7 on 23 degrees of freedom and rejects at 0.05 in 0.018 (the 345 regular samples, unchanged: mean 21.6 on 24, 0.014); moving the fit 4 to 10 units along the diverging direction changes Q1 in the fourth decimal; the bootstrap p-value of the observed Q1 is 0.007 on 400 replicates and 0.06 on the vignette’s 49. Q2 is unchanged: it is computed on every coefficient and its degrees of freedom still count the diverging ones (on the separated samples it rejects in 0.091, on the regular ones in 0.151). Hausman-McFadden and Small-Hsiao are identical on the 400 samples under both builds. In boot_pvalue() a replicate that separates has one degree of freedom fewer than the observed statistic it is compared with.
    • Not changed: two paths of the GMM step on a separated fit (a refused solve() ends the Gauss-Newton loop without a warning; candidates for a later release).
    • Probes: verification/probes/2026-11-12/q1_null.R, q1_mechanism.R, q1_cause.R, hm_null.R and their outputs (q1_null_dir.txt is this design; q1_null_opt3.txt the coefficients-left-out variant it replaced).
  • Log-sum-exp with the row maximum; log P* for the inflated category through a two-term log-sum-exp; plogis/pnorm with log.p for the split equation; 1 - P_ik computed as the sum of the other probabilities.
  • Scale-free checks: the standardization floor is relative to the column’s magnitude (a covariate measured in tiny units is still scaled), and the identification check compares each alternative-specific column’s within-case variation with its own centred sum of squares (a shifted column, w + 1e9, is identified exactly as w is).
  • Probit probabilities below 1e-300 are held at that floor with a zero gradient (the floored log-likelihood is flat), for the bivariate-normal and the GHK paths alike. The remnl mode search runs up to 100 damped Newton steps. The HEV adaptive integration counts the integrals that stop at its panel or depth limit, and the fit warns when any does at the estimate.
  • remnl population-averaged probabilities (no data narrow the integrand): Gauss-Hermite with max(nodes, 7 sigma^2) points per dimension on the 2^k ladder up to 128, then the trapezoidal rule on [-9, 9] standard deviations with a power-of-two number of points at least 18 sigma (step at most 1 / sigma: error about exp(-2 pi^2 / (sigma h)), below 1e-8), so the rule grows linearly in sigma and needs no eigenproblem; Gauss-Hermite rules are memoised. At most 5e4 points in all (or nodes^(J-1)); the fit warns with the error bound when that cap binds (from J = 4 at large sigma).

5. IIA tests: definitions fixed in advance

Hausman-McFadden. Restricted sample: cases with y != d (alternative d dropped), restricted MNL with the same base (or, when d is the base, base c = the first remaining level; the full model is re-expressed with base c by the exact linear map beta_j^(c) = beta_j - beta_c, V^(c) = A V A’). Statistic (beta_r - beta_f)’ (V_r - V_f)^{-1} (beta_r - beta_f) on dim(beta_r) df; vcov = "difference" inverts the difference (Moore-Penrose with a warning when it is not positive semi-definite; negative statistics reported as such with the Hausman-McFadden/Long reading “support for the null”, p-value 1; a positive statistic with an indefinite difference is unreliable, since the form over-rejects); kept as the default because it is the form the literature and Stata’s hausman report; vcov = "joint" uses Var(beta_r - beta_f) = V_r + V_f - C - C’ with the cross term from the stacked per-case scores (suest), positive semi-definite by construction and valid with robust/cluster covariances.

Small-Hsiao. Stratified random half-split (by chosen alternative). Full MNL on half 1 and on half 2: theta_1, theta_2; theta_12 = sqrt(1/2) theta_1 + (1 - sqrt(1/2)) theta_2. Restricted MNL on half 2 without alternative d: theta_r. Statistic -2 [l_2^r(theta_12 restricted to the remaining parameters) - l_2^r(theta_r)] on dim(theta_r) df. The prior project’s lineage (restricted model on both halves, no weighting) is 2 chi-square and is not implemented.

Fok-Paap. Pairs {j, m}: base pairs (J - 1) or all pairs J(J-1)/2. Pairwise binary logit P(y = j | y in {j, m}) = Lambda(V_j - V_m). CL estimator maximises the sum over pairs and cases in the pair of the binary log-likelihood; Godambe covariance (H^{-1} J H^{-1})/n with J from the per-case summed pair scores. Q1 = (theta_ML - theta_CL)’ V_d^{-1} (theta_ML - theta_CL), df = dim(theta) (or the rank of V_d when a generalized inverse is needed). Default V_d (vcov = "joint"): the outer product of the stacked influence functions psi_i = V_ML s_i^ML - H_CL^{-1} s_i^CL (summed by cluster with a cluster), positive semi-definite by construction; vcov = "difference": V_CL - V_ML, F&P eq. 18, indefinite in nearly every sample because the CL estimator is nearly efficient under the MNL (ledger, q1_covariance_check.R). GMM moments g_i = stack over pairs of (1{y_i = j} - Lambda(V_ij - V_im)) 1{y_i in {j, m}} zeta_ijm with instruments zeta = (x_i, w_ij - w_im); efficient GMM from the MLE with the empirical weight matrix (F&P eq. 15): gmm = "two-step" (default; one weight update, Hansen’s standard two-step estimator), gmm = "iterated" (F&P’s practice; warns when the iteration does not settle, which happens with many moments relative to the sample, e.g. pa2006 with 42 parameters and 84 moments); Q2 = n g_bar’ W g_bar at the GMM estimate, df = #moments - dim(theta). Option gmm = "projected": the C-statistic at the MLE, n g_bar’[W - W D (D’ W D)^{-1} D’ W] g_bar, same df.

5.1 New tests: design and Gate 1 (written 2026-10-18, before any code)

Status: designed, not pursued as a paper (author’s decision 2026-10-18, after the prior-work finding below); an implementation in the package is not scheduled. The search for a new IIA test is closed (author’s decision the same day): on one choice set with case-specific covariates IIA is not identified apart from the logit’s functional form (any positive choice probabilities are a logit in utilities log(P_j / P_b)), and a local power envelope (ledger, 2026-10-18; not checked by simulation, by decision) puts the existing tests within a factor of two to four of the best test that knows the direction, Small-Hsiao excepted, while that best test itself needs thousands of cases for moderate violations. Tests that use choice-set variation (the two-data-set idea of McFadden, Tye and Train 1977) or second choices (the rank-consistency tests) exist and fit few political-science data sets.

Source and authority: the author’s validation plan for the link test (2026-09-02, not in this repository) fixes the gates and their pass/fail rules; nothing here changes a rule. This section fixes the definitions for polychoice and records Gate 1 (theory and invariance). Amendments to the plan are marked as such, with the reason, before any result they could affect.

Common setup. An mnl() fit with base b, full choice sets, no fe; e_ij = V_ij - V_ib for j != b, the fitted utility differences from the base (predict(type = "link") minus its base column; they include the generic terms w_ij’ gamma in the long layout). X is the case-specific design (the regressors that carry alternative-specific coefficients).

Link test (L2, the definition polychoice implements). Q_i = all products e_im e_il, m <= l, m, l != b: (J - 1) J / 2 case-specific columns. The augmented model adds Q with alternative-specific coefficients gamma_j to every non-base equation; H0: gamma = 0. LR = 2 (l_aug - l_MNL). Degrees of freedom (J - 1) r, where r is the rank of Q after projecting out the column space of X (weighted by the frequency weights; columns scaled by their norms, singular values above 1e-7 of the largest). The augmented model adds an orthonormal basis of that r-dimensional span, not a subset of the products: the likelihood, and so LR and LM, does not depend on the basis, and a subset is ill-conditioned when two equations’ slope vectors are nearly collinear (the first probe, which kept a pivoted subset, drew divergence warnings in a design with a cosine of -0.995 between two slope vectors; the basis version does not). Score form (L3): the Rao statistic of the same restriction at the MNL fit, LM = s_g’ [I_gg - I_gt I_tt^{-1} I_tg]^{-1} s_g, with the MNL information, which does not depend on y (canonical link), so the observed and expected forms coincide; robust and cluster variants replace the bracket by the outer product of the per-case (per-cluster) scores of the gamma block after partialling out the theta block. J = 2 is refused (IIA is vacuous there). Varying choice sets are refused in the first version (e_ij is undefined for an unavailable j; a definition is a design decision for later). The squares-only variant (L1, Q = {e_im^2}) is not base-invariant (below) and is not exported; verification scripts keep it only to reproduce the September 2026 runs.

Prior work (literature check 2026-10-18; it corrects the September 2026 review’s “not proposed for IIA before”). Murteira and Ramalho (2016, Econometric Reviews 35(4), 515-552, doi:10.1080/07474938.2013.806849; read in the March 2012 preprint, section 4.1.1) augment multinomial-logit-type mean models with “powers and cross-products of all the elements of X beta” in every argument, a RESET-type test that is in substance L2 (their worked versions add own squares only), as LM tests by artificial regression under the multinomial quasi-likelihood, which is the MNL likelihood for 0/1 choices, and report its power against nested-logit and random-parameter designs; they frame it as a general functional-form test, not as a test of IIA, and their simulations are fractional responses. Murteira (2016, Comm. Statist. Theory Methods 45(24), 7367-7375, doi:10.1080/03610926.2014.980518) generalises the goodness-of-link test to multivariate models with multinomial choice as the illustration (abstract only; to be read). McFadden (1987) sets out auxiliary-regression tests for “functional misspecification” of the MNL (abstract only; to be read). McFadden and Train (2000, JAE 15(5), 447-470) give the LM test for mixing through artificial variables in the fitted probabilities (Gate 1b’s random-constant direction), a different test. Not found in the literature checked: the test analysed as a test of IIA, the base dependence of the squares-only form against the invariance of the full quadratic, the rank df, and a maximum-over-nests bootstrap version of McFadden’s nested-logit test (in the check’s reading of the 1981 working paper of Hausman and McFadden, the tests over trees are dependent and no prescription is given; Murteira and Ramalho’s NESTEDg is a joint chi-square over partitions). Any novelty statement is limited to these and waits for McFadden (1987) and Murteira (2016) to be read in full.

What the link test is. With case-specific covariates only, a violation of IIA shows only as a departure of P(y | z) from the multinomial-logit form in z; the test rejects for any such departure, an omitted nonlinearity in z included. It is a functional-form test with power against IIA violations, as the Fok-Paap moments are (Gate 3d measures how much each test reacts to an omitted x^2).

Max-over-nests test (L4). For every admissible nest S (2 <= |S| <= J - 1, the other alternatives singletons; 2^J - J - 2 nests: 3 at J = 3, 10 at J = 4, 25 at J = 5) the McFadden (1987) score statistic LM_S of nested_lm_test(); statistic max_S LM_S, calibrated by the parametric bootstrap from the fitted MNL (the boot_pvalue() machinery); the maximising nest is reported as a direction, not as a test of that nest.

Gate 1a, base invariance (derived). A change of base from b to c maps the index differences linearly and invertibly: e’_j = e_j - e_c (j != b, c), e’_b = -e_c; the MNL fit is equivariant under the same map (the exact re-basing already used for Hausman-McFadden). Homogeneous quadratics in e’ are homogeneous quadratics in e and conversely, so Q and Q’ span the same columns; the augmented models are the same model, and LR, LM, and df are identical. L1 is not invariant: e’_j^2 = e_j^2 - 2 e_j e_c + e_c^2 needs the cross product, which L1 lacks (already at J = 3). Confirmed numerically (verification/probes/2026-10-18/link_gate1a.R, n = 3000, every base): L2’s LR agrees across the four bases to 1e-12 at J = 4 with three covariates (12.689, df 18), while L1’s moves from 2.52 to 7.25 (df 9). L1 and L2 coincide when the squares already span the quadratic forms (J - 1 >= k(k + 1)/2: one or two covariates at J = 4, binary covariates).

Gate 1a’, the degrees of freedom (derived; amendment to the plan’s definitions, written before Gate 2; the probe above finds the derived ranks: r = 6, 1, 3 at J = 4 with three, one, two continuous covariates, r = 1 at J = 3 with two binary covariates). The plan’s df (J - 1)^2 for L1 and (J - 1)^2 J / 2 for L2 count columns, not directions. With e_j = a_j + x’ b_j, e_m e_l = constant + linear in x + (x’ b_m)(x’ b_l): beyond the span of X the products add only quadratic forms in the continuous covariates, at most k(k + 1)/2 of them for k continuous covariates, fewer with binary covariates (x^2 = x) or few equations. The df is therefore (J - 1) times a numerical rank. Check against the September 2026 null runs (300 replications each, the plan’s diagnostics of 2026-09-02, not in this repository, L1): at k_x = 1 the mean statistic is 2.00 (J = 3) and 2.97 (J = 4), the rank df 2 and 3; rejection at 5 percent is 0.050 and 0.047 at the rank df against the 0.007 and 0.000 reported at the column-count df 4 and 9. At k_x = 4 and 8 the two counts agree and so do the rates (0.050-0.077). The “undersized link test at one covariate” of September was the df count.

Gate 1b, local directions (derived; numerical R^2 to follow). Each departure’s score at the MNL point has the form sum_j (y_ij - P_ij) c_ij(z), so its overlap with the link test is the overlap of c with Q after the MNL score is partialled out (residuals are orthogonal to constants and to X at the MLE). * Nested logit, nest S, lambda -> 1: d log P_j / d lambda = -log P_{j|S} - P_S H_S for j in S and -P_S H_S otherwise (H_S the within-nest entropy), so c_ij = -1{j in S} log P_{ij|S}: McFadden’s (1987) artificial variable. For S = {m, l}, -log P_{m|S} = log 2 - d/2 + d^2/8 + O(d^4) with d = e_m - e_l; the constant and linear parts are annihilated by the MNL score, and the quadratic part, (y_m - P_m + y_l - P_l) d^2 / 8, lies in L2’s span (d^2 = e_m^2 - 2 e_m e_l + e_l^2; e_b = 0 when the base is in S). L2 contains the nested-logit direction to second order in the within-nest index difference; L1 contains it only when the base is in the nest. The higher-order terms lie outside the span, which is where L4, the exact direction, gains. * Random alternative-specific intercepts (case level, covariance sigma^2 S0, sigma^2 -> 0): the score in sigma^2 is (1/2) sum_jk S0_jk [(y_j - P_j)(y_k - P_k) - (1{j = k} P_j - P_j P_k)], which with one-hot y equals sum_j (y_j - P_j) c_j with c_j = S0_jj / 2 - sum_k S0_jk P_k: the McFadden-Train (2000) artificial variable for random constants, linear in the fitted probabilities. P is close to affine in z when effects are weak, so this direction is close to the MNL score: random-constant heterogeneity with case-specific covariates is weakly identified whatever the test. It is the direction of the retired Moran moments (residual times fitted probability), whose 10-13 percent power in September is consistent with this. * Heteroskedastic extreme value, scales -> 1: the score has the same form with c a nonlinear function of the index differences (a Gumbel integral); its overlap with Q is computed numerically from the hev() kernel at unit scales (pending). * Multinomial probit correlation: the probit does not contain the MNL, so there is no score at the MNL point (amendment to the plan’s 1b, written before any result: the probit enters only Gate 3’s power runs).

Gate 1c, generated regressors (derived). The gamma score at the fit is s_g = sum_i (y_i - P_i(theta_hat)) (x) Q_i(theta_hat). The derivative with respect to the theta inside Q is sum_i (y_i - P_i) (x) dQ_i/dtheta, whose mean is zero under H0 (the residual is mean-zero given z), so replacing Q(theta) by Q(theta_hat) changes s_g / sqrt(n) by o_p(1); the theta inside P is handled by the partialling in the LM statistic. LR and LM are therefore asymptotically chi-square on the rank df under H0, the condition of Pagan (1984): the generated regressors’ coefficients are zero under the null. Gate 1c’s large-sample check (N = 50,000, mean statistic / df and the 95th percentile) verifies this numerically.

Gate 1d, calibration. Every bootstrap in polychoice is the parametric bootstrap from the fitted null (y regenerated from the fitted MNL with X fixed), so the observed statistic is never exchangeable with the bootstrap draws under the alternative. The plan’s shuffle check (y permuted against x, under which the constants-only MNL is true) and the strong-violation check (p-value to zero as N grows) are run with Gate 2.

Verification on implementation (in addition to the plan’s Gates 2-6): the augmented-model gradient against numDeriv; LR against LM at large n; the base invariance as a regression test; the rank df with one continuous covariate, with binary covariates only, and at k(k + 1)/2 < (J - 1) J / 2.

6. Verification protocol (the standard set by iop and underdisp)

  1. Oracle agreement: mnl() equals nnet::multinom() (coefficients, log-likelihood, covariance) and mlogit::mlogit() (conditional logit with alternative-specific covariates, varying choice sets) to 1e-6 on simulated and bundled data.
  2. Published results: Bagozzi and Marchetti (2017) Tables A.3/A.4 and the log-likelihoods (MNL -2110.59 / BIMNL -2069.97 on pa2006; MNL -553.50 / BIMNL -545.27 on pres2004) reproduce from the bundled data.
  3. Derivatives: analytic gradient and scores against numDeriv on every layout x inflation x link combination; weight-duplication identity; offset identity; re-basing invariance (same log-likelihood and probabilities for every ref).
  4. Parameter recovery on rmnl() data (bias within Monte Carlo error at n = 5000); coverage of analytic and robust intervals.
  5. Tests: HM invariance to the choice of base; HM/SH/Q1/Q2 null rejection rates within [0.03, 0.08] at nominal 0.05 in a 300-replication check on a J = 3, k_x = 4 design (a band fixed before the check was run), with the per-replication statistics saved under verification/.
  6. Adversarial review rounds (simulated referee panel: applied user, econometrician, numerical analyst, reproducibility reviewer) before any release, with every finding logged in verification/ledger.md.
  7. R CMD check --as-cran clean on Windows (local), GitHub Actions matrix, and the sanitizer workflow from underdisp for the C++ (the last two wait for the GitHub repository, which the author has deferred; they are release requirements).

7. Decisions log

  • 2026-10-13 Name: polychoice (polytomous unavailable, CRAN policy).
  • 2026-10-13 Grammar: multipart formula, last part = inflation; long layout via id/alt arguments on a plain data frame (no dfidx dependency).
  • 2026-10-13 Split equation: logit default (the published BIMNL), probit option; inflated category any level, default the base.
  • 2026-10-13 Hessian by finite differences of the analytic gradient (as iop), not analytic, to keep one code path for both models.
  • 2026-10-13 IIA tests take a fitted mnl object (not formula + data), so a test is always on the model the user actually reports.
  • 2026-10-13 Hessian: analytic in C++ after all (the finite-difference Hessian was off by up to 15 percent on TravelMode under an inverted column scaling); one code path still, since the inflated model’s second derivatives are closed-form.
  • 2026-10-13 Standardization: ts = theta * scale, with the within-case standard deviation for alternative-specific columns; boundary flag on |theta * scale| > 15 (effect of a one-SD change).
  • 2026-10-13 Multistart for imnl(): twelve starts (ten on a grid of beta / delta starts plus two challengers of the incumbent) because the inflated likelihood is bimodal on both bundled data sets; n_modes reported.
  • 2026-10-13 Hausman-McFadden default stays the classic variance-difference form (it is what the literature reports), with the psd flag and a pointer to the joint form; in the 60-replication null check the difference form over-rejects (0.12), the joint form is conservative (0.02), Small-Hsiao (0.03) and Q2 (0.05) are at nominal size.
  • 2026-10-13 Fok-Paap with base pairs and case-specific covariates only has no overidentifying restrictions; fp_tests() then reports Q1 only, with a warning (an error when only the GMM test was requested).
  • 2026-10-14 Fok-Paap Q1 default covariance: the joint (stacked influence function) estimate of Var(theta_ML - theta_CL), positive semi-definite by construction; F&P’s variance difference V_CL - V_ML stays available as vcov = "difference". The CL estimator is within a few percent of efficient under the MNL, so the difference of the two separately estimated matrices is indefinite in nearly every sample (44 percent negative statistics, size 0.033 / 0.042 / 0.049 at 1 / 5 / 10 percent); the joint form had 0.015 / 0.062 / 0.112 (verification/q1_covariance_check.R, 1000 replications).
  • 2026-10-14 Small-Hsiao rows carry separated (a fit of the split has diverging coefficients); the summary’s median_p is the chi-square p-value of the median statistic, as in the battery.
  • 2026-10-14 boot_lr_test(): the Vuong row’s normal p-value is NA for the mnl / imnl pair (no valid normal reference at the boundary), as the LR’s chi-square one is; vuong() prints a note for that pair.
  • 2026-11-05 Firth’s penalty (author’s decision, before the release review rounds): firth = TRUE for mnl() and rologit() only, ties included through the expected information of the tie group (the author asked for ties in this version); validated against brglm2, logistf and coxphf (the last through disjoint time windows, since it has no strata); definitions, refusals and the Monte Carlo in section 1, Phase 4.
  • 2026-11-05 (author’s decision, before the review rounds): an exact linear-programming separation check for mnl() and rologit() (lpSolveAPI in Imports; exported separation()), two starts for penalized fits, and the removal of rologit()’s never-ranked-above refusal; section 1, Phase 4b.
  • 2026-11-06 (author’s decision, during the stress battery’s heavy part and before the review rounds):
    • the maximum-likelihood likelihood-ratio forms compare suprema under separation (fixing term_test()’s statistic from where the optimizer stopped);
    • boot_lr_test() for two rologit() fits;
    • priors for mnl() and rologit() (exported coef_prior()).
    Section 1, Phase 4c.
  • 2026-11-06 (author, on the round-5 review and the stress rerun: “Agreed with all decisions/suggestions”):
    • the saddle step;
    • the zero-comparison correction of the separation type and suprema;
    • the boundary step one parameter at a time;
    • bootstrap draws from a separated restricted model’s limit;

Candidates for later releases (author, 2026-11-06 and 2026-11-07; not for this release)

A running list of candidates, not commitments. Each is reviewed before any work starts, and some will not be taken up.

Binary relatives of the inflated multinomial logit

  • The zero-inflated binary logit: imnl() with two alternatives, the inflated category 0 and a logit split,

    P(y = 1) = Lambda(z'gamma) Lambda(x'beta).

    One likelihood under several names:

    • the logistic regression model with a cure fraction (Diop, Diop and Dupuy 2011, Electronic Journal of Statistics 5, 460-483, doi:10.1214/11-EJS616), the primary reference;
    • the one-trial case of the zero-inflated binomial of Hall (2000, Biometrics 56(4), 1030-1039), a model for bounded counts with random effects;
    • the split-population logit of Beger, DeMeritt, Hwang and Moore (2011, SSRN 1773594, unpublished), with the splitting coefficients’ signs reversed (their eqs. 8-9 and 14-15, pp. 36-37);
    • partial observability with independent parts in its logit form (the probit form is Abowd and Farber 1982, Industrial and Labor Relations Review 35(3), 354-367);
    • the two-path “and” Boolean logit (Braumoeller 2003, Political Analysis 11(3), 209-233, doi:10.1093/pan/mpg012).

    Inflating category 1 is the same model for 1 - y. With the same covariates in both parts the likelihood is symmetric in (beta, gamma), so the model is identified only up to exchanging the parts; Tomo, Eguchi and Yoneoka (2026, arXiv:2604.20322) prove this for the logit-logit model, give sufficient conditions for the existence of estimates (double separation) and a relabeling heuristic, and do no inference after relabeling. Diop et al. require a continuous covariate in one part only. With an intercept-only split the model is not identified. So an implementation refuses an intercept-only split and, by default, a shared design; checks for double separation; and starts from asymmetric points that include the exchanged pair.

    A probit split, Phi(z’delta) Lambda(x’beta), is the mirror image of the zero-inflated logit probit model of Pho (2024, Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods 53(18), 6580-6599, doi:10.1080/03610926.2023.2248325), whose eq. (1) is Lambda(w’alpha) Phi(x’mu): a logit split and a probit outcome. Whether a difference in links identifies the parts under a shared design is open (Tomo et al. cover logit-logit only). Software: VGAM zibinomial(), gamlss.dist ZIBI, brms, GLMMadaptive and glmmTMB fit the likelihood; none has the identification checks.

  • The partial-observability bivariate probit (Poirier 1980, Journal of Econometrics 12(2), 209-217, doi:10.1016/0304-4076(80)90007-X): y = y1 y2 with correlated probit parts,

    P(y = 1) = Phi_2(z'gamma, x'beta; rho).

    rho = 0 gives Abowd and Farber’s (1982) model, the probit analogue of the zero-inflated binary logit. Identification needs a covariate excluded from one equation (Poirier 1980). In political science: Przeworski and Vreeland (2002, Political Analysis 10(2), 101-112), on IMF agreements, and Nieman’s strategic probit with partial observability (2015, Political Analysis 23(3), 429-448). Rainey and Jackson (2018, Political Science Research and Methods 6(2), 381-391, doi:10.1017/psrm.2017.3) show by simulation that small misspecifications of functional form bias the estimates badly when a covariate enters both equations. Software: Stata biprobit, partial; GJRM (Model = "BPO", and "BPO0" for rho = 0); BiProbitPartial was archived from CRAN in 2023.

  • Two-sided misclassification of the outcome (Hausman, Abrevaya and Scott-Morton 1998, Journal of Econometrics 87(2), 239-269, doi:10.1016/S0304-4076(98)00015-3). With false-positive and false-negative rates alpha_0 and alpha_1,

    P(y = 1) = alpha_0 + (1 - alpha_0 - alpha_1) F(x'beta),

    constant rates with alpha_0 + alpha_1 < 1, identified through the functional form of F. With alpha_0 = 0 and alpha_1 = 1 - Lambda(z’gamma) it is the zero-inflated binary logit above. The multinomial version replaces the rates by a misreport matrix (Poterba and Summers 1995, Review of Economics and Statistics 77(2), 207-216, with rates from reinterview data; Molinari 2008, Journal of Econometrics 144(1), 81-117, partial identification). imnl() is already the case in which a true j is reported as k with probability 1 - phi(z); a free matrix is identified only by functional form (compare Gate C1 of Phase 3), so validation data or known rates would be needed. In political science: over-reporting a vote for the winner (Atkeson 1999, Political Behavior 21(3), 197-215); Katz and Katz (2010, American Journal of Political Science 54(3), 815-835) correct binary turnout misreports with auxiliary information. Software: logistic4p (binary, constant rates).

Multinomial models

  • A three-level nested logit, extending nlogit()’s two levels (Train 2009, ch. 4; Stata’s nlogit fits more than two levels).
  • The latent-class rank-ordered logit of Fok, Paap and van Dijk (2012, Journal of Applied Econometrics 27, 831-846, doi:10.1002/jae.1223). Latent segments differ in how many ranks a respondent reports reliably; it nests rologit() and allows a likelihood-ratio test of the segments.
  • The multinomial logit with a covariate-dependent scale (heterogeneous choice): the utilities are scaled by a function of respondent covariates, so that choices are more or less predictable from one respondent to the next. Swait and Louviere (1993, Journal of Marketing Research 30(3), 305-314) on the scale parameter; DeShazo and Fermo (2002, Journal of Environmental Economics and Management 44(1), 123-143) parametrize it. Political science has the tradition of Alvarez and Brehm (1995, American Journal of Political Science 39(4), 1055-1082) for binary and ordered choices, and Mauerer and Tutz (2023, Statistical Methods & Applications 32(1), 129-148, doi:10.1007/s10260-022-00642-5) apply a heterogeneous multinomial logit to vote choice (GLES 2017; replication code, no package). It is the respondent-level counterpart of hev(). The scale equation has no constant, and scale and coefficient heterogeneity are confounded when a covariate enters both.
  • The fractional multinomial logit for shares: the MNL quasi-likelihood with shares in place of 0/1 choices (Papke and Wooldridge 1996, Journal of Applied Econometrics 11(6), 619-632, for one fraction; Mullahy 2015, Journal of Econometric Methods 4(1), 71-100, for several), e.g. party vote shares by district, the data that Katz and King (1999, American Political Science Review 93(1), 15-32) and Tomz, Tucker and Wittenberg (2002, Political Analysis 10(1), 66-83) model through log-ratios. Martins and Murteira (2026, “Measuring electoral persistence in multiparty systems: a multivariate fractional regression approach”, CeBER Working Paper 2026-05) fit the dogit, that is imnl(), to vote shares, so a fractional imnl() comes with it. Only sandwich standard errors are valid, and the likelihood-based tools (LR tests, vuong(), AIC, the IIA tests) refuse these fits.
  • The conditional fixed-effects multinomial logit for panels (Chamberlain 1980, Review of Economic Studies 47(1), 225-238, doi:10.2307/2297110; Stata femlogit, Pforr 2014, Stata Journal 14(4), 847-862, with an application to British election panel data). It conditions the unit effects out, avoiding the incidental-parameters bias of unit dummies in short panels. The likelihood conditions on each unit’s choice counts and so needs a recursion over orderings; it yields odds ratios but not probabilities, and units that never change and time-invariant covariates drop out. No R implementation found (2026-11-07).

Features

  • Counterfactual choice sets, elasticities and diversion ratios, with intervals. The question of what would have happened had a party not run (Alvarez and Nagler 1995, American Journal of Political Science 39(3), 714-744; Lacy and Burden 1999, American Journal of Political Science 43(1), 233-255), with simulation intervals (King, Tomz and Wittenberg 2000, American Journal of Political Science 44(2), 347-361), under every family, including those that relax IIA (nlogit, hev, mnprobit, imnl). predict() on long data already drops an alternative whose rows are left out; intervals, an availability argument for wide data, and elasticities are missing. For imnl() the counterfactual has to say what respondents captive to a removed alternative do.
  • Survey designs and multiple imputation. Design-based standard errors (Lumley 2004, Journal of Statistical Software 9(8)) for weighted election studies: polychoice’s weights are frequency weights, and non-integer survey weights are treated as frequency weights. svyVGAM covers the multinomial logit with case-specific covariates only. Probability weights change what the log-likelihood means, so LR tests, vuong() and AIC refuse them or use design-based versions; WESML for choice-based samples (Manski and Lerman 1977, Econometrica 45(8), 1977-1988) comes with them. Multiple imputation (Amelia, Honaker, King and Blackwell 2011, Journal of Statistical Software 45(7); mice): coefficients pooled by Rubin’s rules through tidy(), and pooled quantities of interest.
